Using detergents or sanitisers for the wrong purpose or at the wrong concentration can also harm health or result in inadequate treatment.
paragraphs.procedure: Check the edges and surfaces of tableware and separate defective items from the area of use. When something breaks, also check the effect on nearby food and utensils. Read chemical labels and the restaurant’s work instructions, measure the required amount, and use and store the chemicals as specified.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not use tableware if you cannot adequately confirm whether fragments have stuck to it. Do not decide on your own that a stronger chemical concentration is more effective. Do not spray alcohol near flames, and follow specified conditions such as the moisture on the surface being treated.
paragraphs.scenario: A glass breaks near the plating area. Do not resume work after merely picking up the fragments. Set aside nearby dishes and utensils and report to the person in charge. Stop serving until checks are complete, and clean and take action appropriate to the affected area.

rst-1-cook-18.summary: Check damaged items separately from their effects on the surroundings, and follow specified chemical concentrations and methods of use.
rst-1-cook-18.activity: For a broken-glass situation, list in order the work to stop, the items to separate and the information to report.

rst-1-cook-19.title: Prevent kitchen fires and prioritise evacuation
rst-1-cook-19.objective: Inspect heat sources and electrical equipment, and choose safe actions without attempting dangerous firefighting.

paragraphs.knowledge: Combustible materials near flames, unattended frying oil, damaged cords and dust on sockets can cause fires. Stay at your station while using flames, and handle electrical equipment correctly too. Routinely check where extinguishers and evacuation routes are located.
paragraphs.procedure: Inspect the area around heat sources and electrical equipment before and after work. If you find an abnormality, stop use safely and report it. In a fire, alert those nearby and follow the restaurant’s assigned roles, such as reporting the fire and guiding people. Attempt initial firefighting only within safe limits, and evacuate immediately if the fire is intense.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not touch plugs with wet hands or unplug equipment by pulling the cord. Do not become so absorbed in firefighting that you lose your escape route. If flames are spreading to the ceiling, avoid taking risks; after evacuating, do not return to collect belongings.
paragraphs.scenario: While using the fryer, you are called from the dining area. Do not leave with the oil still heating. Take a safe approach, such as asking another staff member to take over. Also check that nearby cloth, paper and aerosol cans are kept away from the heat source.

rst-1-cook-19.summary: Prevent fires through daily inspections; if a fire occurs, prioritise reporting and evacuation and avoid dangerous firefighting.
rst-1-cook-19.activity: Check how to operate an extinguisher’s safety pin, nozzle and lever, and explain the process, including the decision to retreat safely.

rst-1-cook-20.title: Use the kitchen glossary to cross-check ingredients, tools and methods
rst-1-cook-20.objective: Connect names found in the index with real items’ features and uses, and distinguish homophones and alternative names.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: The same name can refer to different things
paragraphTitles.procedure: Explain the item’s name and when it is used
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not mechanically reproduce source spellings
paragraphTitles.scenario: Prevent tool mix-ups through clear communication

paragraphs.knowledge: Kaki can mean the fruit persimmon or the shellfish oyster; momo can mean a peach or a cut of meat. Cups and ladles are utensil names, not units of quantity in themselves. Tall cylindrical stockpots, yukihira saucepans and woks differ in shape and use; sirloin, rump and tenderloin are meat cuts. Do not finalise orders or preparation based only on pronunciation: check the ingredient category and the actual item.
paragraphs.procedure: Divide the study glossary into ingredients, cuts, cutting styles, cooking methods, machines, utensils and safety. Investigate which dishes use seasonal seafood, vegetables and fruit. Distinguish round slices, half-moon slices and quarter-round slices by shape, and irregular chunks, finely chopped pieces and fine strips by their finished appearance and size. Cross-check tool names against the names used at the restaurant.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not count the same food as different foods because it is listed under different readings. When ordering meat cuts, also specify the animal species. For the index entry written “リブリース” (riburīsu), compare it with the usual beef-cut name “リブロース” (riburōsu) (rib loin) and the diagram in the main text. Do not replace an unfamiliar name with a similar word on your own: check with the person responsible.
paragraphs.scenario: A senior colleague says, “Use the tebo,” but the new worker does not understand. Confirm its purpose, look at the actual basket-shaped tool used for boiling noodles, and repeat the instruction back. In another task, distinguish a food probe thermometer from a thermometer for the inside of a storage cabinet, and say what you will measure before using it.

rst-1-cook-20.summary: Check names, categories, shapes and uses together to prevent mix-ups between ingredients and utensils.
rst-1-cook-20.activity: Review the list for 7 minutes, then spend 8 minutes choosing 5 ingredient terms, 5 utensil terms and 5 cutting-style terms. Spend 8 minutes explaining them as if using actual items or original diagrams, then spend 7 minutes organising alternative names, homophones and inconsistent spellings in the source material.

rst-1-hyg-16.title: Read and write hygiene plans and implementation records
rst-1-hyg-16.objective: Record what was checked, when and how, and what was done when an abnormality occurred.

paragraphs.knowledge: A hygiene plan sets out in advance when and how to check things and what to do if there is a problem. Implementation records document that day’s checks and responses. Check both general hygiene management and the important controls for each dish, and use the results for reflection and improvement.
paragraphs.procedure: Read your assigned items and checking times, and fill in the record only after actually checking. For temperatures, record the value and unit; for abnormalities, record the food name, time, circumstances, response and person notified. If you notice a missing entry, establish the facts and follow the restaurant’s correction procedure.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not mark all the satisfactory boxes before work or record another person’s checks as your own. Writing only “abnormality found” does not let the next person decide what to do. Also check that actual work matches the method in the plan.
paragraphs.scenario: A delivered bag was torn, so you requested a replacement. Record not just the defect but which product and how many units you separated, whom you informed and what action was taken. Provide information that prevents the next person from mistakenly using items still awaiting action.

rst-1-hyg-16.summary: Distinguish plans from records and leave a traceable account of verified facts and responses to abnormalities.
rst-1-hyg-16.activity: Create one sample record for a normal day and one for a day with a temperature abnormality, and hand them over to another learner.

rst-1-svc-01.title: Understand customer expectations and QSCA
rst-1-svc-01.objective: Observe food, service, cleanliness and atmosphere and choose actions for improvement.

paragraphs.knowledge: Customer satisfaction relates to the gap between expectations and actual experience. QSCA covers four aspects: food quality, customer service, cleanliness and atmosphere. Taste, portion size, presentation, appropriate temperature, speed and staff responses together form one experience.
paragraphs.procedure: Inspect your assigned area from all four perspectives. Check food finish and serving order, and notice customers’ expressions and waiting times. Address dirt or missing supplies when you notice them, and give the responsible person specific information about anything you cannot resolve yourself.
paragraphs.mistakes: A smile alone cannot make up for long waits or the wrong dish. Likewise, rushing by omitting explanations or seating guests at a dirty table harms the experience. Avoid making customers feel pressured by watching them continuously; respond when needed.
paragraphs.scenario: Food preparation is on schedule, but customers are waiting at the entrance to be seated. Do not focus only on your own task: acknowledge their wait and speak to them. Tell the responsible staff member the party size and waiting situation so they can be seated.

rst-1-svc-01.summary: Look at the whole restaurant from four perspectives and improve the experience customers receive.
rst-1-svc-01.activity: Imagine entering a restaurant as a customer. Give one good point and one improvement for each QSCA aspect.

rst-1-svc-02.title: Prepare your greeting, appearance and bow
rst-1-svc-02.objective: Express welcome or apology with a clean appearance and calm movements.

paragraphs.knowledge: Greetings begin customer service. Use a voice that reaches the listener, a gentle expression and an upright posture. Choose a bow for its purpose: about 15 degrees for a light bow, 30 degrees for a formal bow and 45 degrees for a deeply respectful bow. More than the angle, it matters to stop and bow carefully.
paragraphs.procedure: Check your hair, nails, clothes, shoes and accessories and tidy your appearance. Face the customer to greet them and bow from the upper body, rather than bending only your neck. Give way to customers in passages and keep enough distance to avoid collisions even when carrying a tray.
paragraphs.mistakes: Avoid leaning against a wall or speaking with your arms folded. Strong scents and conspicuous accessories may affect dining or hygiene. Do not use the same loud voice with everyone; adapt to the listener’s hearing and the restaurant environment.
paragraphs.scenario: A customer calls you while you are busy. Rather than turning around and answering as you walk, stop in a safe place to respond. If you cannot come immediately, acknowledge them and connect them with the responsible staff member.

rst-1-svc-02.summary: Greet people in a way suited to them, with a clean appearance and courteous movements.
rst-1-svc-02.activity: Divide up three situations: arrival, passing someone and apologising. Check one another’s voice, posture and bow.

rst-1-svc-03.title: Handle trays, glasses and plates safely
rst-1-svc-03.objective: Check where to touch tableware and its centre of gravity, and carry dishes steadily.

paragraphs.knowledge: Support a tray near its centre with your non-dominant hand and keep its weight balanced. Hold glasses lower down, away from the rim that touches the mouth. Keep fingers away from the parts of a plate that contact food or the mouth, and place the dish with its presentation side facing the customer.
paragraphs.procedure: Check for damaged tableware and confirm that the tray is stable. Put heavy items in stable positions, such as nearer you; do not place tall items at an unstable edge. Check the route, carry the dishes, alert the customer and quietly set the tableware down from a safe position.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not make carrying a large quantity at once your priority. Tilting an unstable tray above or near a customer’s head is dangerous. Also avoid holding glass rims, plate interiors or the parts of cutlery that touch the mouth.
paragraphs.scenario: A child suddenly stands up in the passage. Do not try to squeeze past; stop and maintain a safe distance. Tell people nearby that you are carrying hot food, and ask another staff member to check the route if necessary.

rst-1-svc-03.summary: Check balance and hygienic points of contact, and serve without carrying more than you can manage.
rst-1-svc-03.activity: Plan how to arrange tableware of different weights on an empty tray, and explain where to support it and the order for setting items down.

rst-1-svc-04.title: Understand Japanese meal layout and seating
rst-1-svc-04.objective: Understand the basic layout of one soup and three dishes and the serving sequence, and serve according to restaurant policy.

paragraphs.knowledge: For a meal of one soup and three dishes, the basic arrangement puts rice on the left and soup on the right, with the main dish, side dishes and pickles arranged around them. A kaiseki banquet meal may proceed through appetisers, clear soup, sashimi, simmered or grilled dishes, fried dishes, vinegared dishes, rice and fruit. Confirm the actual menu and order at your restaurant.
paragraphs.procedure: Check the menu and sample place setting, and align dish orientation and tableware positions. In a Japanese-style room, know where the entrance and decorative alcove are, and follow guests’ preferences and the seating policy. Handle chopsticks hygienically and prepare the utensils needed for sharing dishes.
paragraphs.mistakes: Even if you know the principles of seats of honour and lower-status seats, do not decide someone’s job rank or age from appearance when seating them. Guests’ preferences and ease of movement may take priority. Check dish orientation from the guest’s side, rather than the server’s.
paragraphs.scenario: For a reservation in a Japanese-style room, a guest requests a seat near the entrance. Do not insist on the formal seat of honour. Confirm the request and tell the responsible person. Check that seating and food service will work before showing the guest to the seat.

rst-1-svc-04.summary: Learn the basic arrangement and sequence, and adapt them to the actual menu and guests’ wishes.
rst-1-svc-04.activity: Draw the positions of rice, soup, main dish, side dishes and pickles, and explain the serving sequence for kaiseki banquet cuisine.

rst-1-svc-05.title: Western-style cutlery and meal progress
rst-1-svc-05.objective: Check cutlery arrangements and respond without assuming whether a customer is still eating.

paragraphs.knowledge: In Western-style dining, knives go on the right and forks on the left, with knife blades facing inward. When several utensils are needed, arrange them from the outside in according to their order of use. The positions of knives, forks and napkins give clues to meal progress, but asking the customer also matters.
paragraphs.procedure: Check the courses and the restaurant’s serving method, and set out clean cutlery. Serve in line with the progression of soup, fish, meat, dessert and other dishes. Replace dropped utensils rather than asking customers to pick them up.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not decide the meal is finished and clear plates simply because utensils have been placed together. The side from which food and drinks are served can differ by restaurant and service style. In cramped seating, do not force your body into the space; confirm a safe method.
paragraphs.scenario: A customer has left the seat with food still on the plate. Do not clear it just because the seat is empty. Look at meal progress and the napkin and check with the responsible staff member. When the customer returns, ask whether they will continue eating before acting.

rst-1-svc-05.summary: Know basic arrangements and clues to meal progress, and confirm customers’ wishes before serving or clearing.
rst-1-svc-05.activity: Arrange a knife, fork and soup spoon, and explain how their placement differs during a meal and when it has finished.

rst-1-svc-06.title: Serve safely at a Chinese round table
rst-1-svc-06.objective: Understand round-table seating and sharing practices and prevent turntable accidents.

paragraphs.knowledge: In Chinese dining, guests may share dishes from large platters, and some restaurants use a turntable. The basic seat of honour is on the side farthest from the entrance. Changing individual plates for each dish also helps prevent flavours from mixing.
paragraphs.procedure: Check the number of people, dishes, individual plates and serving utensils. Before moving the turntable, use words and visual checks to make sure nobody is taking food. Keep glasses and personal chopsticks off the turntable and serve dishes in a stable condition.
paragraphs.mistakes: Even if you know the usual direction of rotation, suddenly turning without checking the surroundings can knock dishes over. Do not impose seating customs or the practice of leaving food on every customer. Respond according to their wishes and the restaurant’s service method.
paragraphs.scenario: As you are about to put a platter on the turntable, the customer opposite is taking food. Do not turn it immediately. Wait until they finish and speak to them. Especially with hot dishes, make sure there is enough space to avoid contact with hands or tableware.

rst-1-svc-06.summary: At a turntable, check the movements of others and handle individual plates and dishes safely.
rst-1-svc-06.activity: Imagine six people at a round table. Practise the checks and verbal warnings needed when placing dishes and turning the table.

rst-1-svc-08.title: Manage food from completion to service and takeaway
rst-1-svc-08.objective: Serve food promptly and accurately explain the restaurant’s storage conditions and consumption deadline for takeaway.

paragraphs.knowledge: Food remains affected by time and temperature after cooking is complete. Serve hot items in an appropriate condition and cold items promptly while maintaining their temperature. Taking home leftovers and takeaway prepared for sale may involve different processes and restaurant policies.
paragraphs.procedure: Confirm the dish, table and order requirements before serving. If there is a wait, store the food as instructed. For takeaway requests, ask the person in charge whether the dish can be taken away, and convey the restaurant’s specified information about containers, storage and when to eat it.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not give blanket assurances such as “anything is safe within two hours”. Conditions vary with the dish, temperature and time since cooking. Even to reduce food waste, do not decide on your own to hand over food that cannot hygienically be taken away.
paragraphs.scenario: A customer wants to take home food that has been on the table for a long time. Do not immediately hand over a container. Check the dish and elapsed time and consult the person in charge. If the request cannot be met, explain why politely and do not invent a storage deadline.

rst-1-svc-08.summary: Maintain control until service, and check and accurately explain takeaway conditions.
rst-1-svc-08.activity: For a takeaway request, write separately the information you must check and the information you must tell the customer.

rst-1-svc-09.title: Confirm orders and make recommendations politely
rst-1-svc-09.objective: Use basic expressions appropriately and clearly confirm orders and suggestions.

paragraphs.knowledge: Service expressions have different roles: irasshaimase welcomes a guest, kashikomarimashita acknowledges a request, and mōshiwake gozaimasen apologises. Beyond politeness, clearly communicate what you have agreed to do.
paragraphs.procedure: Ask the party size and preferences, and repeat the product names, quantities and changes to confirm. Before recommending something, understand the dish’s features accurately and suggest options suited to the customer’s wishes. If an item is sold out or a request cannot be met, state the facts and check alternatives.
paragraphs.mistakes: Speak clearly, avoiding unnecessary “no hō” wording or past-tense expressions layered onto a present confirmation. When handing over a receipt, use a concise expression such as “Reshīto de gozaimasu” (Here is your receipt). Do not repeatedly push a recommendation after it is declined.
paragraphs.scenario: A customer wants fish, but today’s fish is sold out. Do not vaguely accept the order: apologise and explain that it is unavailable. Before suggesting an alternative, also check their preferences and foods they cannot eat.

rst-1-svc-09.summary: Combine basic expressions with specific confirmation to obtain accurate orders and make appropriate suggestions.
rst-1-svc-09.activity: Practise four situations: confirming party size, repeating an order, explaining a sold-out item and responding when a recommendation is declined.

rst-1-svc-10.title: Take telephone reservations and messages accurately
rst-1-svc-10.objective: Listen, repeat back and hand over information politely when you cannot see the caller’s expression.

paragraphs.knowledge: On the telephone, neither person can see the other’s expression. State the restaurant’s name and your own, and listen calmly. Do not guess anything you miss: confirm and record it. Accurately pass requests you cannot decide yourself to the responsible person.
paragraphs.procedure: Introduce yourself and ask the purpose of the call. For reservations, confirm date, time, party size, name, contact details and necessary requests. Repeat important numbers and details. If putting the caller on hold or calling back is necessary, explain why and how contact will be made. Give the record to the responsible person and confirm follow-up.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not leave unheard names or dates blank. Never assume conversations cannot be heard while someone is on hold, or make promises you have not checked. Also keep your voice at a level that avoids unnecessarily disclosing the caller’s personal information to others nearby.
paragraphs.scenario: A caller says “next Friday”. Confirm and repeat the specific month and date to avoid confusion. If you do not know seat availability, check with the responsible person rather than confirming the booking immediately.

rst-1-svc-10.summary: Repeat dates and numbers, and record matters you cannot decide yourself for the responsible person.
rst-1-svc-10.activity: Role-play a reservation call and demonstrate how to clarify and repeat back information you cannot hear clearly.

rst-1-svc-11.title: Respond reliably to food-allergy questions
rst-1-svc-11.objective: Check ingredients and preparation processes and involve the person in charge without giving unverified safety assurances.

paragraphs.knowledge: Food allergies can cause not only rashes and nausea but also severe symptoms such as difficulty breathing or changes in consciousness. Checks must cover not just visible ingredients but also sauces, processed ingredients and cross-contact through shared utensils.
paragraphs.procedure: Ask which ingredient the customer needs checked, and consult the person in charge and kitchen staff about the latest ingredient information and preparation process. Accurately explain what was verified, what cannot be accommodated and the possibility of cross-contact. Record the order conditions and share them with cooking and serving staff.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not decide on your own that removing a visible ingredient is enough. Do not guarantee “it definitely contains none” based only on an old recipe or memory. Distinguish the labelling system for processed foods from information restaurants provide about their dishes.
paragraphs.scenario: A customer avoiding milk asks about a soup. Even if no dairy is visible, check the seasonings used in preparation. If ingredients or processes cannot be verified, do not describe it as safe; ask the person in charge to respond.

rst-1-svc-11.summary: Check current ingredients and processes, and accurately communicate verified facts and the limits of what can be accommodated.
rst-1-svc-11.activity: Imagine taking an order to avoid egg. Organise the information to convey to the customer, cooking staff and serving staff.

rst-1-svc-12.title: Alcoholic drinks and checks before serving
rst-1-svc-12.objective: Distinguish fermented and distilled drinks and perform necessary age and driving checks.

paragraphs.knowledge: Fermented drinks include wine, beer and sake; distilled drinks include brandy, whisky, gin and shōchū. Knowing ingredients and production methods helps with explanations. However, check each product’s alcohol content and ingredients against its label and restaurant information.
paragraphs.procedure: When taking an alcohol order, follow restaurant procedures for necessary age verification and checking whether the customer plans to drive a car, ride a bicycle or operate another vehicle. Do not serve alcohol to people under 20 or those who will drive. Ask the person in charge to handle difficult decisions.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not infer that someone is at least 20 simply because they say they are an adult. Do not rely only on appearance or companions’ answers: check the required identification. Also clarify who is the designated driver in a group.
paragraphs.scenario: A customer planning to cycle home orders beer. Do not assume it is acceptable because they are not driving a car. Refrain from serving alcohol and inform the person in charge. Offer a non-alcoholic drink available at the restaurant instead.

rst-1-svc-12.summary: Describe products accurately and check that alcohol is not served to those under 20 or those who will drive.
rst-1-svc-12.activity: Give two examples each of fermented and distilled drinks, and practise verification and refusal when a customer’s age is unknown.

rst-1-svc-13.title: Nutrients and the five basic tastes
rst-1-svc-13.objective: Use the main functions of nutrients and differences in taste to give basic dish descriptions.

paragraphs.knowledge: Protein, fat and carbohydrates are the three major nutrients. Adding vitamins and minerals gives the five major nutrient groups. Protein builds the body, while fat and carbohydrates provide energy. Vitamins and minerals help regulate bodily functions, among other roles.
paragraphs.procedure: Check main ingredients such as meat, fish, eggs, soy products, rice, bread, noodles, vegetables and fruit. Organise tastes as sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami and connect them with the restaurant’s descriptive terms. Use verified information to answer questions about nutrient quantities.
paragraphs.mistakes: One ingredient does not contain only one nutrient. Also, do not classify spicy and hot-temperature sensations together with the five basic tastes. Staff must not independently guarantee treatment or health benefits concerning an individual’s condition or dietary restrictions.
paragraphs.scenario: A customer asks whether a dish is low in salt. Do not answer that it is based only on your own taste. Ask kitchen staff what information the restaurant can verify and whether adjustments are possible. Avoid making individual health judgements.

rst-1-svc-13.summary: Understand basic nutrition and taste, and base quantity and health-related explanations on verified information.
rst-1-svc-13.activity: Choose a set meal and explain which ingredients relate to the five major nutrients and which basic tastes you notice in its dishes.

rst-1-svc-14.title: Respect dietary diversity when advising customers
rst-1-svc-14.objective: Respect religious and dietary differences and ask specifically which foods a person cannot eat.

paragraphs.knowledge: Halal refers to what is permitted under Islamic law. Vegetarian and vegan approaches also differ in the foods avoided and underlying views. Do not judge dietary preferences from appearance, nationality or name; ask the person what conditions they need.
paragraphs.procedure: Ask about ingredients they cannot eat and conditions concerning stock, seasonings, cooking utensils and similar matters. Check dish ingredients and processes with the person in charge and explain what can be accommodated. Even when suggesting alternatives, verify the changed ingredients before recommending them.
paragraphs.mistakes: A dish without visible meat may still contain meat stock or fish ingredients. Not using pork alone does not justify guaranteeing halal suitability. Do not assume everyone has the same restrictions without asking the person’s conditions.
paragraphs.scenario: You are about to recommend vegetable soup to a vegan customer. First check whether the stock or seasonings contain animal-derived ingredients. If the restaurant cannot meet requests such as separate utensils, explain this honestly in understandable language.

rst-1-svc-14.summary: Do not judge by a label alone. Match the person’s conditions against the dish’s ingredients and process before advising them.
rst-1-svc-14.activity: Create three specific questions each for a customer requesting halal food and for a vegan customer.

rst-1-svc-15.title: Connect opening preparation with closing work
rst-1-svc-15.objective: Perform before- and after-service checks in order and hand over unfinished work.

paragraphs.knowledge: Before opening, check cleaning, supplies, tableware, reservations, seats, change and staff roles. After closing, carry out the restaurant’s requirements, such as cleaning, replenishment, settlement, disposal, equipment checks and locking up. Connect preparation and tidying with the next day’s service in mind.
paragraphs.procedure: Check the checklist and assignments, and inspect dining areas, entrance, toilets, serving equipment and till. Cross-check reserved dishes and seating with kitchen staff too. At closing, consider customers’ circumstances, complete the required tasks after their departure and tell the person in charge what remains unfinished.
paragraphs.mistakes: A tick on a checklist does not guarantee supplies are complete. Check actual quantities and condition. Do not start noisy cleaning immediately beside customers simply because closing time has passed. Do not omit safety checks such as checking heat sources.
paragraphs.scenario: Just before opening, you notice one seat is missing for a group booking. Do not force an extra chair into a passage. Confirm the reservation and layout with the person in charge. Prepare while keeping passages needed for evacuation and serving clear.

rst-1-svc-15.summary: Check actual items, prepare for service and safety, and hand over unfinished matters.
rst-1-svc-15.activity: Create opening and closing checklists and assign responsibilities for reservations, supplies, till and safety.

rst-1-svc-07.title: Ask people what assistance they need
rst-1-svc-07.objective: Ask guests with children, older guests and guests with disabilities about their wishes and guide them appropriately.

paragraphTitles.supportMarks: Use symbols as a starting point for assistance

paragraphs.knowledge: The support needed differs from person to person. Do not assume what someone can or cannot do based only on age, a wheelchair, appearance or a symbol. Ask the person about their wishes and adjust passages, seating, menu visibility and communication methods such as speech or writing.
paragraphs.procedure: Ask the person, “Is there anything I can help you with?” Check seats usable while remaining in a wheelchair, passage width and changes in floor level. Obtain consent before helping with movement. Provide children’s seats and tableware or menus easier for older guests to read as needed.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not touch wheelchairs or assistance dogs without permission, or speak only to companions instead of the person. Do not automatically refuse assistance dogs as if they were pets; guide admission according to restaurant procedures. If unsure, involve the person in charge.
paragraphs.scenario: A guest showing an ear symbol requests written communication. Do not simply continue speaking louder. Check available methods such as paper or a device. Show the order details and price directly to the guest and confirm understanding.
paragraphs.supportMarks: Assistance-dog, ear, ostomate, Heart Plus, Help Mark and maternity symbols, among others, offer clues about support or facilities. Understand their meanings, then ask what help is needed without casually asking detailed medical diagnoses. Assistance dogs include guide dogs, mobility assistance dogs and hearing dogs. Do not feed or distract a dog while it is working.

rst-1-svc-07.summary: Avoid assumptions: ask the person what they want and find a method the restaurant can provide.
rst-1-svc-07.activity: Practise the initial questions and guidance to a seat in three situations: a party with children, a wheelchair user and someone who has difficulty hearing.

rst-1-svc-16.title: Keep dining and shared spaces clean
rst-1-svc-16.objective: Choose tools and a sequence suited to the area and check the condition visible to customers.

paragraphs.knowledge: Dining areas, toilets and staff spaces become dirty in different ways. Use separate cleaning tools for each area. Cleaning is not just making something clean once: maintaining that condition matters. Check dirt visible from a seated position and deterioration of fixtures too.
paragraphs.procedure: Prepare so cleaning does not affect food or customers. Generally work from high places downward. Remove dry dust appropriately and pre-treat stubborn dirt according to the material and detergent. Afterwards, wash the tools and inspect the area at seated eye level too.
paragraphs.mistakes: Continuing to wipe with a dirty cloth can spread dirt. Never use toilet tools on tables. Include less visible places and air-conditioning filters in the plan, and report torn carpets or equipment abnormalities.
paragraphs.scenario: The table has been wiped, but food remains in a gap in the chair. Do not declare the work complete after looking only from above: check from the sitting position too. Ensure the surrounding area is clean and safe before seating the next customer.

rst-1-svc-16.summary: Follow the area-specific tools and plan, and check cleanliness from both the worker’s and customer’s perspectives.
rst-1-svc-16.activity: Imagine choosing one seat. List the high-to-middle-to-low cleaning sequence and the places to check after sitting down.

rst-1-svc-17.title: Check cash and cashless payments
rst-1-svc-17.objective: Match amounts with the payment method to prevent duplicate payments and incorrect change.

paragraphs.knowledge: Cash includes 10,000-, 5,000-, 2,000- and 1,000-yen notes, and 500-, 100-, 50-, 10-, 5- and 1-yen coins. Cashless methods include credit cards, debit cards, electronic money and code payments. Available methods differ with the restaurant’s contracts and terminal.
paragraphs.procedure: Check the bill, order and total and ask the payment method. For cash, state the amount received and check the change and receipt before handing them over. When using a terminal, follow restaurant procedures and verify the payment result before saying payment is complete.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not repeatedly process a payment without checking the result just because the terminal is unresponsive. Check the restaurant’s result, not only the customer’s screen. Do not treat old note illustrations or brand names in materials as the entire current range: use the restaurant’s latest guidance.
paragraphs.scenario: Communication stops after a code payment. Do not immediately accept cash and close the transaction. Ask the person in charge to check payment status. To prevent double payment, share the result and response before explaining them to the customer.

rst-1-svc-17.summary: Check the total, amount received, change and payment result, and do not repeat processing on a guess before completion.
rst-1-svc-17.activity: Practise a cash transaction paying 3,200 yen with 5,000 yen, and a terminal transaction with an unknown payment result.

rst-1-svc-18.title: Receive complaints and reports of foreign objects
rst-1-svc-18.objective: Listen to the customer, preserve the actual item and facts, and report accurately to the person in charge.

paragraphTitles.prevention: Prevent foreign objects in dining areas too

paragraphs.knowledge: Complaints arise from dissatisfaction with food, waiting times, service and other matters. First listen to the whole account and establish what happened. Hard foreign objects can cause injury, and even parts of ingredients such as bones can be a problem. Prioritise checking health and safety.
paragraphs.procedure: Apologise, ask about the situation and the customer’s condition, and stop serving the dish if needed. Do not discard the object or dish: preserve them according to restaurant procedures and tell the person in charge and kitchen staff the table, dish, time and complaint. Confirm authority and the customer’s wishes before replacement, refund or similar action.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not jump to conclusions about the cause or argue that the customer is at fault. Never remove only the object and return the same dish. Do not end with words of apology alone: inform the person in charge about other affected dishes and equipment too.
paragraphs.scenario: A customer reports a hard transparent fragment in a dish. Check for injury, preserve the item and call the person in charge. Share any knowledge of tableware breaking nearby and have possible effects on other dishes checked.
paragraphs.prevention: Prevent doors being left open and rubbish being left out; act when you notice insects or dirty fixtures. Clean air-conditioning filters and similar equipment regularly. Avoid clips, staples, pencils and other easily introduced objects near food. Appearance checks and checking supplies for damage also help prevent foreign objects.

rst-1-svc-18.summary: Check the account and the person’s condition, preserve the item and facts, and involve the person in charge.
rst-1-svc-18.activity: Role-play receiving a foreign-object complaint. Check the first words to say, handling of the item and information to report.

rst-1-svc-19.title: Respond to a customer becoming suddenly unwell
rst-1-svc-19.objective: Ensure safety, communicate symptoms and arrange necessary emergency help and restaurant coordination.

paragraphs.knowledge: There are many causes of illness during a meal, and restaurant staff alone cannot diagnose them. When there is urgency, such as breathing difficulty, unusual consciousness or food choking, prioritise emergency assistance and calling for help. Food allergies can suddenly cause severe symptoms.
paragraphs.procedure: Make the surroundings safe and call the person in charge and other helpers. In an emergency, call 119, describe the location, symptoms, consciousness and breathing, and follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions. Assign separate roles for attending the person, guiding responders and making the call, and clear the responders’ access route.
paragraphs.mistakes: Never force water or food on someone who is unconscious or has difficulty swallowing. Do not dismiss a dangerous condition as something that will improve with a little rest. Do not improvise procedures you have not been trained in; follow emergency instructions and the procedures you have learned.
paragraphs.scenario: After eating, a customer reports difficulty breathing. Do not wait until the cause has been fully investigated: call for assistance and emergency help. Communicate the food eaten, time of onset and symptoms as far as you can confirm them, and stay with the person while monitoring their condition.

rst-1-svc-19.summary: Prioritise safety and emergency assistance over identifying the cause, and coordinate according to instructions.
rst-1-svc-19.activity: In a practice 119 call, check the order for giving the restaurant’s location, symptoms and contact details.

rst-1-svc-20.title: Guide customers safely during earthquakes and fires
rst-1-svc-20.objective: Protect yourself first, then follow the restaurant’s role assignments and evacuation plan.

paragraphs.knowledge: Disaster preparation must happen before a disaster occurs. Routinely check evacuation routes, assembly points, heat sources, emergency reporting and support for people needing assistance. Falling and broken objects are earthquake hazards; smoke and spreading flames are fire hazards.
paragraphs.procedure: During strong shaking, protect yourself and call on those nearby to stay safe. When shaking stops, assess the situation and guide people according to the restaurant plan. For fire, alert others and coordinate emergency reporting, initial firefighting and evacuation guidance among assigned staff. Count people after evacuation.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not pass through dangerous areas to put out a fire or return for belongings after evacuating. In areas at risk of tsunami, confirm evacuation to predesignated high ground or other safe places. Keeping evacuation exits free of objects is also part of daily preparation.
paragraphs.scenario: After an earthquake, broken glass is near the entrance. Rather than rushing everyone toward the same exit, confirm a safe route with the person in charge and guide them in a calm voice. Ask the wishes of people needing help to move and coordinate with helpers.

rst-1-svc-20.summary: Check evacuation plans routinely and coordinate with priority on your own and customers’ safety when a disaster occurs.
rst-1-svc-20.activity: Mark two evacuation routes and an assembly point on a restaurant plan. Assign and practise emergency calling, guidance and head-count roles.

rst-1-hyg-17.title: Distinguish heating conditions for eggs and liver
rst-1-hyg-17.objective: Distinguish conditional egg exceptions from the ban on serving liver raw, and heat food to the centre using the restaurant’s verified procedures.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Eggs have a heating rule and conditional exceptions
paragraphTitles.procedure: Separate liver freshness from suitability for eating raw
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not extend exceptions based only on appearance
paragraphTitles.scenario: Match customer requests with kitchen standards

paragraphs.knowledge: For dishes using hen eggs, a benchmark is heating the whole food at 70°C for at least 1 minute. Exceptions may apply when sound eggs intended for raw consumption, within their date and free of dirt or shell cracks, are cooked promptly, among other conditions. The date alone does not establish suitability for raw consumption. Do not stockpile cracked-open eggs for a long time: handle the amount needed just before use.
paragraphs.procedure: Beef liver and pork, including offal, cannot be sold or served for raw consumption. The teaching example heats the centre to 75°C for at least 1 minute. Equivalent disinfection methods such as 63°C for at least 30 minutes are also specified for beef liver, but do not substitute improvised low-temperature cooking: follow the restaurant’s validated process. Separate utensils used before and after heating too.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not include cracked or dirty eggs among sound eggs for raw consumption simply because they are within date. Do not use hen-egg conditions to guarantee safety for all egg products or all customers. “Fresh liver” or “the customer requested it” does not justify serving it raw. Surface colour alone cannot replace checking centre temperature and holding time.
paragraphs.scenario: A customer requests liver cooked rare. Rather than passing this directly to the kitchen for execution, explain that the item is served cooked through to its centre. Another worker finds a cracked egg, keeps it separate from normal eggs and consults the person in charge. Judge the order, ingredients and heating record separately.

rst-1-hyg-17.summary: Apply egg exceptions only when all necessary conditions are met, and do not serve beef or pork liver and similar products for raw consumption. Check temperature at the food’s centre.
rst-1-hyg-17.activity: Read for 8 minutes, then spend 7 minutes classifying three cases: an in-date cracked egg, a sound egg intended for raw consumption and beef liver. Spend 8 minutes explaining checks of centre temperature and holding time, then 7 minutes practising replies that do not extend exceptions without justification.

rst-1-hyg-18.title: Connect hygiene terms with tasks and hazards
rst-1-hyg-18.objective: Organise and explain hygiene-index terms by their roles in causes, prevention, checks and records.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Distinguish the purposes of similar words
paragraphTitles.procedure: Sort the index into four categories
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Check similar readings against real differences

paragraphs.knowledge: Washing removes dirt; disinfection targets pathogenic microorganisms. Killing microorganisms, general cleaning and drying are not synonymous either. Cross-contamination describes contamination transferring to another food through food or utensils; secondary contamination also describes food becoming contaminated again after processing. Show what transferred from where to where, rather than only naming it.
paragraphs.procedure: Using the study glossary, place bacteria, viruses, parasites, pesticides and hard foreign objects in the hazards category, and handwashing, low-temperature control and heating in countermeasures. Put thermometers, centre temperature and control standards under checks, and daily logs, records and special notes under records. If a term relates to multiple categories, explain why.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not treat refrigerator interior temperature, food centre temperature and infrared-measured surface temperature as the same. Hard glass fragments and soft foreign objects such as hair cause different hazards. Do not call hepatitis E virus, norovirus, roundworms and Anisakis collectively bacteria. The glossary is a starting point for verification, not a substitute for safe action.
paragraphs.scenario: A new worker reports only “the temperature is strange”. A senior colleague asks what was measured, with which instrument, at what time and against which standard. The new worker selects the necessary index terms and explains, “The refrigerator’s interior temperature exceeded the restaurant’s upper limit. It is recorded, and the food is awaiting checks.”

rst-1-hyg-18.summary: After learning how to read a term, explain in a workplace sentence what it is used to protect.
rst-1-hyg-18.activity: Read for 7 minutes, spend 8 minutes selecting 15 glossary terms and sorting them into four categories, then 8 minutes explaining differences between three pairs of similar terms. Use the remaining 7 minutes to create a handover containing numbers and facts.

rst-1-svc-21.title: Connect service terms with ordering, serving and payment
rst-1-svc-21.objective: Select necessary terms from the service index and distinguish customer-facing expressions from kitchen work terms.

paragraphTitles.procedure: Use terms to make short confirmation sentences
paragraphTitles.mistakes: A name alone does not guarantee availability or suitability
paragraphTitles.scenario: Rephrase specialist terms for the listener

paragraphs.knowledge: Customer satisfaction, expectations and hospitality describe the experience; serving, clearing and table setting describe actions. Bill payment concerns confirming what is being paid, while settlement concerns correctly processing and balancing amounts. Even for similar words, check the restaurant’s roles and actual tasks, and choose expressions customers can easily understand.
paragraphs.procedure: Select glossary words related to seats, dishes, drinks, dietary conditions, payment, support and safety. Organise seats of honour and lower-status seats as seating positions, and main and side dishes as meal roles. Learn mobility assistance, hearing and guide dogs as assistance-dog categories, and ask the person what accommodation is needed. Also compare drink names and payment methods with actual products and menus.
paragraphs.mistakes: Halal, vegan and allergy do not mean the same restrictions. Do not complete Japan’s alcohol-serving age check merely by asking whether someone is an adult. Even if you know terms for breathing difficulty or sudden illness, do not diagnose the condition yourself: seek help according to the restaurant’s emergency procedure.
paragraphs.scenario: When kitchen staff say “get the main dishes for the same table ready together”, the worker confirms that the intention is to serve that table’s food together. Do not use internal abbreviations unchanged with customers; explain when their food will be served. For payment questions, check the restaurant’s guidance on accepted cards and electronic methods before replying.

rst-1-svc-21.summary: Connect term meanings with tasks and give customers verified information in words they understand.
rst-1-svc-21.activity: Read for 7 minutes and spend 8 minutes sorting glossary terms into seven categories. Practise customer-facing and kitchen-facing confirmation sentences for a combined 8 minutes, then rewrite ambiguous abbreviations for 7 minutes.

rst-2-hyg-11.title: Manage recalls, transport and sales
rst-2-hyg-11.objective: Trace affected items when problems emerge after sale, and manage temperatures and labelling during transport and display.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Manage food after it leaves the restaurant too
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not return recalled goods to normal stock
paragraphTitles.scenario: A label omission in delivered products

paragraphs.knowledge: Prepare for voluntary recall of problematic food by defining the person responsible, product identification, customer contact, reporting to public health authorities and separation of recalled items. Deciding to recall and filing a notification when a recall starts are separate actions; check current official guidance for scope and procedures.
paragraphs.procedure: Clean vehicles and containers and pre-cool where necessary before loading. Load and unload quickly and check temperature and time through arrival. During sale, follow storage conditions on labels or instructions and stay below refrigerated display-case load limits. Stop sales and respond to delivery abnormalities or errors in dates or allergen labels.
paragraphs.mistakes: Clearly identify and isolate returned or recalled food to prevent resale. Cooling a product after arrival does not erase temperature deviations during delivery. Identify the time of the abnormality and affected lot and retain the basis for action. Also investigate whether loading with non-food goods could cause contamination.
paragraphs.scenario: An ingredient-label omission is found on packaged products already delivered. The person in charge stops sales of the same lot and checks destinations and quantities in the records. Assign a contact person and storage location for recalled products, and check whether official reporting is required and how to do it. Track recall progress and label-check methods to prevent recurrence.

rst-2-hyg-11.summary: Prepare in advance for stopping sales, tracing affected items, making contact and isolating recalled products.
rst-2-hyg-11.activity: Read for 8 minutes and create a delivery checklist in 7 minutes. Spend 8 minutes arranging recall steps after a label omission is found, and 7 minutes designing affected-lot and customer-contact records.

rst-2-hyg-12.title: Verify the effectiveness of records and training
rst-2-hyg-12.objective: Use records for cause analysis and training improvement and check actual behaviour changes.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not fill in normal values later

paragraphs.knowledge: Recording purchasing, manufacturing and cooking, shipping and sales, and in-house inspection results enables tracing warning signs and affected food. Use daily inspection records to prevent incidents, investigate causes and improve work. Sample inspection forms help organise checks, but filling in the same form is not the goal itself.
paragraphs.procedure: Adapt training to assigned work, covering health management, clothing, handwashing, food and utensil separation and chemical handling. After explaining, ask the worker to demonstrate and reteach what they cannot do. Assign recorders and checkers and retain the abnormality, action, decision-maker and recheck results.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not enter unmeasured values from memory or erase abnormality records. If entries are often missing, do more than warn individuals: examine measuring locations, form placement and workload. Do not treat attendance as proof of competence; observe behaviour in actual work.
paragraphs.scenario: Everyone completed video training, but some still choose the wrong chopping board. The supervisor uses actual equipment to check storage locations and use labels. Improve unclear labels and ask each person to choose and explain equipment. Verify improvement through observations the following week and feed results into training.

rst-2-hyg-12.summary: Use records and training to discover abnormalities and improve actions.
rst-2-hyg-12.activity: Read for 8 minutes, examine a fictional temperature record for 7 minutes and create additional abnormality entries in 8 minutes. Use 7 minutes to decide what a new worker should demonstrate and how to check one week later.

rst-2-hyg-13.title: Manage preparation, thawing and uncooked-food processes
rst-2-hyg-13.objective: Design work areas and sequences to prevent contamination of food that will not be heated.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Whether food will be heated later changes the hazard
paragraphTitles.procedure: Adapt when areas cannot be separated
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Room-temperature thawing and unplanned simultaneous work

paragraphs.knowledge: Preparing raw meat, fish and soil-covered vegetables can spread contamination. Food not heated afterwards, such as salad or sashimi, cannot have attached microorganisms reduced by cooking. The person in charge defines task-specific utensils, covered containers, areas and sequence and separates prepared food from untreated ingredients.
paragraphs.procedure: Do clean tasks such as preparing food for raw consumption first, then wash and disinfect equipment and utensils when changing tasks. Plan thawing under low-temperature conditions suitable for the ingredient, collecting drips so they cannot fall on other food. Refrigerator, running-water and microwave thawing differ in time, uneven temperature and quality effects: choose according to product instructions and subsequent steps.
paragraphs.mistakes: Prolonged room-temperature thawing can let surface bacteria grow even while the centre stays frozen. Do not plate salad beside raw-meat preparation or wipe contaminated and clean areas with the same cloth. Washed vegetables can become contaminated afterwards too, so keep them covered and refrigerated.
paragraphs.scenario: Repairs reduce available worktops. The supervisor changes the plan to finish salad preparation first, cover and refrigerate it, then process raw meat. Define separate utensils and cloths and who cleans at changeover. If the planned quantity cannot be made safely, reduce the number served rather than force simultaneous tasks.

rst-2-hyg-13.summary: Separate ingredients, utensils, times and areas and protect food that will not be heated through the final step.
rst-2-hyg-13.activity: Read for 8 minutes and create an order of work for limited worktops in 8 minutes. Spend 7 minutes explaining thawing-method choices and 7 minutes practising changeover checks.

rst-2-hyg-14.title: Cooling, storage and plating after cooking
rst-2-hyg-14.objective: Manage subsequent temperature history and recontamination as well as heating conditions.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: A single temperature check is not enough

paragraphs.knowledge: Manage heating principles according to ingredients and processes: heat the centre at 75°C for at least 1 minute, or shellfish and similar foods at risk of norovirus contamination at 85–90°C for at least 90 seconds. Spore-forming bacteria can survive normal cooking, so prevent food being left standing and plan cooling, storage and reheating.
paragraphs.procedure: Measure with a food probe thermometer and check time after the required temperature is reached. Cooling guidelines for large-scale catering are around 20°C within 30 minutes or around 10°C within 60 minutes; check applicability and equipment capacity when planning. Maintain at least 65°C during hot holding of cooked food. Do not confuse this with the 60°C used in general explanations of preventing microbial growth.
paragraphs.mistakes: One temperature measurement is not the end of control. Do not cool a large pot for a long time at room temperature or pack hot food into a refrigerator so it warms other food. Prepare clean worktops, utensils, containers and gloves for plating; after another task, wash hands and change gloves appropriately. If gloves or utensils are damaged, also check for fragments in food.
paragraphs.scenario: More bookings led to more stew, but its temperature at the planned time was outside the standard. The person in charge holds the food and decides action from its temperature history. Next time, review division into shallow containers and cooler-use sequence and assign measurement duties. Do not prepare quantities beyond cooling capacity in advance.

rst-2-hyg-14.summary: Check cooking, cooling, hot holding and plating as a continuous process and distinguish where each standard applies.
rst-2-hyg-14.activity: Read for 8 minutes and examine cooking and cooling records for 8 minutes. Create a portioning plan suited to equipment capacity in 7 minutes, then explain holding decisions for deviations and recontamination prevention in 7 minutes.

rst-2-cook-01.title: Assess meat and fish quality
rst-2-cook-01.objective: Judge acceptance and use by matching specifications with temperature history rather than declaring safety from appearance alone.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not serve after surface checks alone
paragraphTitles.scenario: The same meat gives a different result

paragraphs.knowledge: Meat cuts differ in fat and connective tissue, affecting texture even with the same cooking method. Seafood deteriorates differently by type and size. Colour, springiness, smell and drips provide clues to quality, but freshness alone cannot guarantee absence of pathogens or parasites.
paragraphs.procedure: Check delivery specifications and actual goods and promptly store meat in the temperature range suited to its category and seafood in the range suited to the item. Collect thawing drips so they cannot fall on other food. Combine texture-suited methods, such as stewing connective-tissue-rich meat or briefly cooking tender cuts, with safe heating conditions.
paragraphs.mistakes: Cook formed meat thoroughly to its centre. Fresh fish is not necessarily suitable for sashimi: confirm raw-consumption specifications and controls. Leave pufferfish preparation to staff meeting the required qualifications, authorisation and facility conditions. General staff must not imitate the process themselves.
paragraphs.scenario: A new delivery has more connective tissue and becomes tough with the usual grilling method. The supervisor checks changes in cut and specifications and trials a method meeting quality standards. Do not weaken safety conditions to prioritise tenderness; return to the original specification if needed. Reflect changes in recipes and customer explanations too.

rst-2-cook-01.summary: Choose cooking methods by considering ingredient features, specifications, storage history and safety conditions together.
rst-2-cook-01.activity: Read for 8 minutes and compare cooking plans for two meats in 7 minutes. Practise a fish acceptance decision for 8 minutes, then explain in 7 minutes why quality observations alone cannot guarantee safety.

rst-2-cook-02.title: Explain vegetables and Japanese-produced ingredients
rst-2-cook-02.objective: Check ingredient characteristics and labels to choose storage methods and customer explanations.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not store or heat everything alike
paragraphTitles.scenario: The day the origin label changes

paragraphs.knowledge: Vegetables contain much water, and the edible part varies: leaf, root, stem or fruit. Cooking reduces volume but can also leach water-soluble components and change colour. Traditional vegetables connect with regional food culture. Wagyu is a breed-based name and does not mean all cattle raised in Japan.
paragraphs.procedure: Check leaf firmness, skin, weight and deterioration by item. Distinguish those suited to cool, dark storage from those needing refrigeration, and prevent drying and transpiration. Separate leaves and roots of leafy root vegetables when needed. Base origin, variety and brand descriptions on delivery documents and labels, avoiding vague names.
paragraphs.mistakes: Preserving green-leaf colour, preventing lotus-root or burdock discolouration, and drawing out moisture with salt serve different purposes. Preparation affects texture and nutrition too, so do not universally instruct prolonged soaking. Do not label traditional vegetables or wagyu based only on appearance or price.
paragraphs.scenario: The origin of a vegetable used in the same dish changes. The shift leader matches documents to actual goods and updates the information board. Because firmness differs, trial cutting and heating methods and share procedures that meet finished-product standards. Also check that staff are no longer introducing it under the former origin.

rst-2-cook-02.summary: Choose handling suited to ingredient characteristics and verify origin and variety explanations against labels.
rst-2-cook-02.activity: Read for 8 minutes and create a storage table for three vegetables in 7 minutes. Spend 8 minutes listing what must be updated after an origin change, then explain wagyu versus Japanese-raised beef in 7 minutes.

rst-2-cook-03.title: Standardise preparation quality and work sequence
rst-2-cook-03.objective: Teach preparation with both taste and hygiene in mind and reduce variation in results.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not sacrifice safety for appearance

paragraphs.knowledge: Washing, removing bitterness, scoring and rehydrating dried ingredients improve flavour and ease of eating. At the same time, prevent dirt and microorganisms in ingredients spreading to the next step. Teaching why a process is done, as well as the finished form, helps workers adapt to ingredient changes.
paragraphs.procedure: Spread leafy vegetables’ leaves to remove dirt and wash soil-covered vegetables in a dedicated area. Locate and cut meat sinews; remove fish scales, gills and viscera as required for the use. Scoring positions differ for whole fish with head and tail and for portions. After washing under running water, promptly remove moisture and refrigerate appropriately.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not leave ingredients at room temperature during preparation or touch finished food with hands used to gut fish. Separate knives and worktops and wash and disinfect at changeovers. Check necessity and quality effects before pounding ingredients strongly or soaking them for a long time.
paragraphs.scenario: A new worker’s fish portions differ in thickness, raising concern about uneven cooking. The instructor shows the finished-weight and thickness standards and checks the first portion together. Record trimming losses and teach knife use and ingredient positioning. Do not rush the learner to work alone before they can do it safely.

rst-2-cook-03.summary: Teach preparation with its purpose, finished standard, contamination prevention and storage included.
rst-2-cook-03.activity: Read for 8 minutes, classify preparation purposes in 7 minutes and explain fish-processing steps in 8 minutes. Spend 7 minutes planning demonstrations for beginners and checks for passing.

rst-2-cook-04.title: Create cooking plans and finished-product standards
rst-2-cook-04.objective: Organise multiple orders’ processes to meet safety, quality and service-time requirements together.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Consider how each method heats food
paragraphTitles.procedure: Prepare by working backwards from orders
paragraphTitles.mistakes: A larger quantity may need different conditions

paragraphs.knowledge: Boiling, simmering, steaming, grilling, frying and stir-frying differ in heat transfer, moisture and oil quantities. Hygiene is especially important when mixing, dressing or chilling food without subsequent heating. Set finished-product standards for portion size, plating, serving temperature and time, as well as taste.
paragraphs.procedure: Set preparation quantities from sales forecasts and check staff and equipment availability. Begin time-consuming steps first and coordinate kitchen and dining staff so dishes for one table are ready together. Recipes should state ingredients, portions, sequence, storage deadline, equipment and safety precautions and be accessible when needed at work.
paragraphs.mistakes: Larger loads in a pot or fryer change temperature recovery and cooking time. Simply increasing heat in a rush enlarges the difference between outside and inside. Follow item-specific holding times and storage conditions for advance preparation; do not make more than demand and postpone temperature control.
paragraphs.scenario: Orders for dining groups overlap and the grill station falls behind. The supervisor organises steps and tells dining staff which dishes can go first and which must be served together. Rather than suddenly assigning untrained people to dangerous equipment, use them to help plate or prepare. Review preparation amounts and equipment layout afterwards.

rst-2-cook-04.summary: Plan backwards from completion, considering demand, staff, equipment and holding conditions together.
rst-2-cook-04.activity: Read for 8 minutes and create a schedule for serving three dishes to one table in 8 minutes. Explain staffing changes during a rush in 7 minutes and inspect portion and holding-time checkpoints in 7 minutes.

rst-2-cook-05.title: Find kitchen equipment abnormalities early
rst-2-cook-05.objective: Use checks of heating, cooling and washing equipment to decide when to stop use or arrange maintenance.

paragraphTitles.procedure: Opening and closing checks for the model
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not hide faults by changing settings
paragraphTitles.scenario: A dishwasher fails during the rush

paragraphs.knowledge: Even with a temperature set, dirt or faults can reduce actual performance. Inadequately ventilated gas equipment risks carbon monoxide poisoning; dirty refrigerator seals and heat-dissipating parts affect cooling. Dishwashers work effectively only when nozzles, hot-water supply, detergent supply and other systems function correctly.
paragraphs.procedure: Follow the manual to check ignition, ventilation, temperature, leaks and damage. Beware hot steam from steam equipment; confirm cooling and power shutdown before cleaning. Check ice-machine interiors and scoop storage too. Check fryer oil condition and the restaurant’s replacement criteria and report abnormalities to the person in charge.
paragraphs.mistakes: Lowering the setting of a refrigerator that is not cooling does not identify the cause or establish food history. Do not try to compensate for poor washing by cramming in dishes. Temperature requirements vary by model and detergent, so prioritise your own manuals and management plan over another restaurant’s values.
paragraphs.scenario: Dishwasher rinsing becomes inadequate during a rush. The supervisor separates processed and unprocessed tableware and does not use uncertain items. Check safely according to the manual and arrange repair. Define an alternative process that reliably washes and disinfects, assess service capacity and reduce sales quantities if needed.

rst-2-cook-05.summary: Check actual equipment performance rather than settings, and protect food and workers when abnormalities occur.
rst-2-cook-05.activity: Read for 8 minutes and create refrigerator and dishwasher checklists in 7 minutes. Decide tableware separation and alternative processes for a breakdown in 8 minutes, and organise information for the manufacturer in 7 minutes.

rst-2-cook-06.title: Manage utensil materials and measurement accuracy
rst-2-cook-06.objective: Teach care suited to use and material and prevent incidents and losses from breakage or measurement errors.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Choose utensils by purpose and material
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Moving scales is also a checking opportunity

paragraphs.knowledge: Match blades to tasks and foods: yanagiba for sashimi, deba for fish preparation, nakiri or usuba for vegetables and petty knives for fine work. Materials require different care even when shapes match. Scale and thermometer accuracy affects portions, costs and heating decisions, so visible cleanliness alone is insufficient.
paragraphs.procedure: Separate knives and chopping boards by use, then wash, disinfect and dry after use. Remove dirt along board grooves and store where air reaches all surfaces. Wash fluoropolymer-coated pots with tools that do not damage the surface and avoid rapid cooling. Remove moisture from iron items according to instructions to prevent rust.
paragraphs.mistakes: After moving a scale, check level and operation and use it on a stable surface. Errors such as including container weight or confusing g and kg disrupt recipes and costs. Stop use on finding metal-scourer fragments, peeling pot surfaces or chipped utensils, and check for contamination of food too.
paragraphs.scenario: Costs rise and the supervisor finds container weight was not being subtracted. Check scale operation and units, then demonstrate taring. Have the worker repeatedly weigh the same amount and another checker verify it meets the standard. Add checks for introducing new containers too.

rst-2-cook-06.summary: Care for utensils according to material and coordinate units, tare and operation checks when measuring.
rst-2-cook-06.activity: Read for 8 minutes and match knife uses with care in 7 minutes. Demonstrate weighing with a container in 8 minutes and explain the scope of checks for damaged utensils in 7 minutes.

rst-2-cook-07.title: Anticipate workplace injuries and change the layout
rst-2-cook-07.objective: Make fall, cut, burn and entanglement hazards visible and improve work methods.

paragraphTitles.scenario: Repeated near misses in a passage

paragraphs.knowledge: Wet floors, loads blocking vision, workers passing with hot containers and unattended blades create overlapping kitchen hazards. The person in charge must improve passages, lighting, load size, storage, protective equipment and training rather than rely on attention alone. Rotating machinery parts and blades are also major hazards.
paragraphs.procedure: Show slippery locations, hot equipment and blade storage on maps or procedures. Remove water and oil promptly and use trolleys or multiple people for heavy loads. Check cooling and other safety conditions when changing oil or handling steam equipment. Stop machines for cleaning or clearing jams and follow manuals and restart-prevention procedures.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not permit use with safety covers removed, hands put into rotating parts to save time, or blades hidden in sink water. A warning sign alone does not remove the hazard. Stop work if it cannot be done safely and carry out needed repairs or layout changes.
paragraphs.scenario: A pot carrier and clearing worker nearly collide at the service hatch. The supervisor observes movement during the rush and changes carrying direction and temporary storage. Assign someone to remove floor droplets and practise warnings for hot loads. Observe the same period afterwards to check whether danger has decreased.

rst-2-cook-07.summary: Combine signs, equipment, methods, layout and training, reducing hazards before work.
rst-2-cook-07.activity: Read for 8 minutes and make a kitchen hazard map in 8 minutes. Practise responses to machine jams and carrying hazards for 7 minutes, then decide how to check improvement effectiveness in 7 minutes.

rst-2-cook-08.title: Understand distribution and food additives
rst-2-cook-08.objective: Compare purchasing routes and check additive purposes and conditions of use.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not judge only by natural origin

paragraphs.knowledge: Food arrives through producers, shippers, wholesale markets, processors, retailers and others. Markets support collection, price formation, settlement, information, hygiene and disaster-time supplies. Compare suppliers on specifications, delivery, cold-chain control and traceability as well as price. Central kitchens and specification-based ordering also affect the division of store work and quality control.
paragraphs.procedure: Additives are classified as designated additives, existing additives, natural flavourings and ordinary food additives. Their uses differ, including sweetening, colouring, preservation, antioxidant action, emulsifying, thickening, raising and coagulation. Check permitted foods, amounts and other conditions against product labels and current standards. Item counts and administrative responsibility can change, so do not fix old textbook figures as permanent facts.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not assume natural means safe without limits or preservatives remove the need for temperature control. Do not confuse additive functions with a guarantee of the whole food’s safety: follow labels, use standards and storage conditions. When suppliers change, update specifications, ingredients and allergen information and align customer explanations too.
paragraphs.scenario: A wholesaler suggests a cheaper sauce. The supervisor compares package quantity, usage, storage, delivery, additive and allergen labels as well as unit price. Trial it against finished-product standards; if approved, update recipes and guidance before introduction.

rst-2-cook-08.summary: Understand purchasing conditions and additive purposes and check labels and specifications before making changes.
rst-2-cook-08.activity: Read for 8 minutes and compare two purchasing routes in 7 minutes. Classify additive uses in 7 minutes and explain checks for introducing a replacement sauce in 8 minutes.

rst-2-svc-01.title: Observe QSCA and improve service
rst-2-svc-01.objective: Find specific shortcomings in quality, service, cleanliness and atmosphere and instruct staff on improvement.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Check the gap between expectations and reality
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not stop at abstract warnings
paragraphTitles.scenario: Food is rated highly but repeat visits are few

paragraphs.knowledge: Customer satisfaction is not decided by taste alone. Shortcomings in food quality, service, cleanliness or atmosphere can fall below expectations. The person in charge observes movements and surroundings visible from customer seats and models good service. Staff greetings and teamwork also affect customer treatment.
paragraphs.procedure: Check food portions, temperature and service time, order waits, tableware cleanliness, toilets, lighting, air conditioning and sound levels. Observe posture, walking and consistency of words and expressions and give specific corrections. Follow restaurant standards for Japanese, Western and Chinese serving sequences and utensils, adjusting to meal progress.
paragraphs.mistakes: “Be nicer” or “be faster” alone does not say what to change. Running does not necessarily make serving faster and increases collision and burn risks. Before clearing dishes, do not judge by appearance alone: appropriately confirm the customer has finished without causing discomfort.
paragraphs.scenario: Despite high food ratings, repeat visits are low. The manager observes post-order waits and the dining area rather than rechecking taste alone. Persistent payment queues and uncleared dishes lead to defined responsibilities and signals for assistance. After a week, compare wait times and customer feedback to see whether non-food aspects improved too.

rst-2-svc-01.summary: Turn QSCA into concrete observation points, then instruct and verify effects.
rst-2-svc-01.activity: Read for 8 minutes and make a QSCA observation sheet in 7 minutes. Rewrite vague instructions into specific prompts in 8 minutes, then explain how to measure effects in 7 minutes.

rst-2-svc-02.title: Coordinate accommodation and serving one table together
rst-2-svc-02.objective: Confirm customer wishes and coordinate seating, utensils and serving times as a team.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: The same response does not fit everyone
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not choose support based on appearance
paragraphTitles.scenario: The passage to the reserved seat is narrow

paragraphs.knowledge: Wheelchair users, guests with assistance dogs and parties with children need different accommodations. The manager knows available seats, passages and utensils and asks the person’s wishes. Serving one table’s dishes together and helping children eat earlier should be balanced according to the situation.
paragraphs.procedure: Before choosing seats, ask about movement and seating preferences and share only necessary information with kitchen and service staff. Remove wet floor patches and obstacles and prepare needed plates and cutlery. Check progress for the table; for takeaway, coordinate handover time with storage and eating instructions.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not move a wheelchair without asking or treat assistance dogs uniformly as ordinary pets. Avoid making children’s dishes too early and leaving them standing. Do not leave finished food for a long time merely to synchronise service: ask the kitchen to adjust start times and progress.
paragraphs.scenario: A wheelchair user arrives and the planned seat proves difficult to reach. The supervisor asks their wishes and offers a more accessible seat. Clear the route and tell the kitchen the changed table number. Also ask whether the child’s food should come first and assign responsibilities so service for everyone stays coordinated.

rst-2-svc-02.summary: Confirm personal wishes, movement safety and meal progress and align the team’s responses.
rst-2-svc-02.activity: Read for 8 minutes and choose an accessible seat from a floor plan in 7 minutes. Practise asking wishes on arrival for 8 minutes and organise coordination points for table service and takeaway in 7 minutes.

rst-2-svc-03.title: Teach service expressions and recommendations
rst-2-svc-03.objective: Teach suggestions and telephone responses that suit customers’ wishes using clear words and expressions.

paragraphTitles.procedure: Give a brief demonstration on the spot
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Avoid vague assurances and pressure selling
paragraphTitles.scenario: Reservation party sizes do not match

paragraphs.knowledge: Service language conveys welcome, confirmation, explanation and thanks. Alongside polite forms, align understandable content, voice volume, expression and eye contact. Recommendations help customers choose suitable dishes and combinations, rather than forcing extra orders.
paragraphs.procedure: When you notice a slip or unclear response, demonstrate a specific expression and ask the worker to say it again. Recommendations must accurately state quantity, price, ingredients and serving timing. On the telephone, clearly give the restaurant name and purpose; repeat and record dates, times, party size, contact details and other important points because the caller cannot see you.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not promise unverified waits or allergy accommodations. Do not repeat the same suggestion after refusal; respect the customer’s purpose for the meal. Instead of scolding a new worker at length in front of guests, make necessary corrections then practise somewhere calm.
paragraphs.scenario: A reservation record says four people, but arriving guests say six. The manager listens and checks available seats.
