Afterwards, review questioning with the telephone worker and add a final combined repeat-back of date, time and number. Verify through demonstration and check the next reservation record too.

rst-2-svc-03.summary: Teach accurate information, clear speech and respectful suggestions by example.
rst-2-svc-03.activity: Read for 8 minutes and role-play a telephone reservation for 8 minutes. Create a recommendation explanation in 7 minutes and turn vague phrases into specific guidance in 7 minutes.

rst-2-svc-04.title: Priorities during busy periods and customer information
rst-2-svc-04.objective: Organise competing requests around safety and quality and share customer information appropriately.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Observe the whole operation and assign help

paragraphs.knowledge: When routine tasks overlap, prioritise serving finished food and adjust payment, seating and orders to circumstances. Safety incidents such as accidents or sudden illness are a separate priority. Acknowledge customers and explain waits while the manager allocates help according to kitchen and dining-area bottlenecks.
paragraphs.procedure: Add thanks when greeting returning guests and share seating and food preferences only as needed. Define personal-data purposes, access rights and storage and prevent unattended papers or devices. If food is delayed, verify the reason and expected timing and coordinate customer explanations with staffing.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not apply priorities mechanically: a collapsed customer in a passage takes precedence over ready hot food. Do not leave paying customers waiting without acknowledgment or discuss a regular’s preferences or address where other customers can hear. Prevent copying customer data to personal devices or using it for other purposes.
paragraphs.scenario: Food for three tables is ready while customers wait at the till and entrance. The supervisor assigns one worker to serving and personally acknowledges and handles payment. Explain the wait at the entrance and seat guests once a table is ready. Afterwards, record where congestion began and review the next staffing plan.

rst-2-svc-04.summary: Prioritise safety, deploy people according to quality and waits, and keep customer-data handling to the minimum necessary.
rst-2-svc-04.activity: Read for 8 minutes and prioritise a situation with five simultaneous requests in 8 minutes. Practise explanations for 7 minutes and explain appropriate personal-data sharing in 7 minutes.

rst-2-svc-05.title: Answer questions about dietary restrictions and date limits
rst-2-svc-05.objective: Check ingredient, equipment and date conditions and explain in light of dietary wishes and safety.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Dish names and heating alone do not guarantee suitability

paragraphs.knowledge: Food allergies, religious restrictions and vegetarian diets differ, and avoided ingredients and acceptable limits vary by person. Check sauces, stocks, seasonings and shared pots and utensils. For alcohol, follow laws and restaurant procedures for age and driving checks and consistently explain refusals where service is prohibited.
paragraphs.procedure: Use-by dates concern safety, while best-before dates concern quality retention; both assume unopened storage according to the stated method. After opening, follow the restaurant’s conditions and use period. The manager checks dates, storage and opening records together and does not independently serve expired products.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not assume heating an alcohol-containing seasoning necessarily meets a customer’s wishes. Vegetarian dishes may still contain animal-derived stock or gelatin. Do not dismiss an unusual taste complaint as preference: if spoilage or chemical contamination is possible, do not taste it; stop service and examine processes and ingredients.
paragraphs.scenario: A customer wants to avoid animal ingredients. Before suggesting vegetable soup, the worker checks stock, oil and seasonings with the supervisor. Explain shared utensils too, and state what is verified and what cannot be accommodated. Help the customer decide without vague absolute guarantees.

rst-2-svc-05.summary: Verify dietary restrictions and date limits in concrete terms and provide accurate information for customer decisions.
rst-2-svc-05.activity: Read for 8 minutes and compare date decisions before and after opening in 7 minutes. Practise asking about ingredient restrictions for 8 minutes, then explain alcohol checks and unusual-taste responses in 7 minutes.

rst-2-svc-06.title: Inspect opening, closing and dining-area cleaning
rst-2-svc-06.objective: Set responsibilities and completion standards for preparation, closing and routine cleaning and hand service over safely.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not standardise all dilution ratios or times
paragraphTitles.scenario: The next morning’s worker finds poor preparation

paragraphs.knowledge: Opening work prepares surroundings and staff to welcome guests. Closing work checks food storage, money, fire and security and hands over to the next day. Train cleaning with specific tools, steps, scope, finish and frequency, rather than appearance alone.
paragraphs.procedure: Before opening, check air conditioning, lights, equipment, supplies and attendance and contact absent staff. At closing, coordinate last orders with the kitchen and check remaining food, till differences, heat sources, locks and security systems. Use area-specific tools for tables, chairs, supplies and toilets and separately record daily, weekly and monthly schedules.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not apply an example dilution ratio from one cleaning manual to another product: follow its label. Demonstrate proper mop and glass-tool use. Do not leave wet floors without warning, and keep customer routes open. Set equipment preheat times according to model and service plans too.
paragraphs.scenario: The closing list says complete, but seasoning containers and chair undersides remain dirty. The supervisor establishes differing understandings of cleaning scope and shows targets and finished examples. Revise the process so the worker repeats cleaning and someone else checks. Provide handover space for the next shift to report shortcomings.

rst-2-svc-06.summary: Align responsibilities, scope, conditions and completion checks for opening, closing and cleaning before handover.
rst-2-svc-06.activity: Read for 8 minutes and make an opening/closing checklist in 8 minutes. Explain cleaning completion standards in 7 minutes and practise reporting absences and cleaning shortcomings to the next shift for 7 minutes.

rst-2-svc-07.title: Manage till differences and sales money
rst-2-svc-07.objective: Reconcile cash and cashless records and handle discrepancies and deposits securely.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Both shortages and excesses are problems
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not fill gaps from your wallet

paragraphs.knowledge: Cash below recorded amounts causes a store loss, while excess may mean errors such as change owed to customers. For cashless cancellations and refunds, check both terminal operation and sales records. Traceable records explaining discrepancies matter more than simply balancing the total.
paragraphs.procedure: Check change preparation and shortage procedures and train new payment methods. After closing, the responsible worker and checker reconcile actual cash, till records, cancellations, refunds and money movements. Stores using a night safe follow security procedures for designated bags, deposit slips and multiple-person checks, and store next-day change separately.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not conceal shortages with personal money or carry surplus cash to another day. Do not recharge based only on a failed-payment screen: verify transaction status to prevent duplicate payments. Avoid telling unrelated people sales amounts, storage locations or transport times.
paragraphs.scenario: At closing, actual cash exceeds records. The supervisor checks change, cancellations, refunds and interim deposits in order and reports the discrepancy as found. If a change error is identified, follow store procedures and practise error-prone operations with the worker. Do not vaguely carry it over to tomorrow.

rst-2-svc-07.summary: Do not hide discrepancies: investigate causes through records and handle money and payment information according to security procedures.
rst-2-svc-07.activity: Read for 8 minutes and solve a till-record and cash reconciliation example in 8 minutes. Practise duplicate-payment prevention explanations for 7 minutes and organise deposit checks and security procedures in 7 minutes.

rst-2-svc-08.title: Direct initial responses to complaints and emergencies
rst-2-svc-08.objective: Secure health and safety first, record facts, actions and causes separately and prevent recurrence.

paragraphTitles.scenario: A hard fragment is found on a plate

paragraphs.knowledge: Complaints offer clues for service improvement, but foreign objects and illness can directly harm health. The manager first checks the customer’s condition and safety and listens without interruption. Distinguish facts, wishes and the restaurant’s actions without asserting unverified causes. Build a system where staff can report even small complaints.
paragraphs.procedure: Stop serving suspected contaminated dishes and preserve actual items and related information. Check injuries and symptoms and make necessary emergency calls and manager notifications. If consciousness or breathing is abnormal, follow 119 instructions and trained procedures and divide duties such as arranging an AED. Assign other people to secure the area and assist other guests.
paragraphs.mistakes: Remaking food without investigating the contamination route allows recurrence. Do not discard evidence or blame the customer. Avoid independent actions such as forcing an unwell person to stand or giving food or drink. Do not make medical judgements: follow emergency instructions. After the initial response, share causes and countermeasures with all staff.
paragraphs.scenario: A guest reports something unusual in their mouth and a hard fragment is found. The supervisor checks for injury and arranges preservation of food and fragment. Hold other dishes prepared with the same utensils and inspect for chips. Explain to the guest, make necessary contacts and keep response records. Once the cause is known, revise utensil-check timing and replacement criteria.

rst-2-svc-08.summary: Secure safety and make necessary calls first, then preserve items and records and verify causes and countermeasures.
rst-2-svc-08.activity: Read for 8 minutes and practise listening to a complaint for 7 minutes. Make role assignments for finding a foreign object in 8 minutes and explain 119 calling and AED arrangements for sudden illness in 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-01.title: Shift-leader decisions and reporting
rst-2-ops-01.objective: Confirm authority and run planning, execution, evaluation and improvement while maintaining QSCA and hospitality.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not chase profit as a single number
paragraphTitles.scenario: Equipment fails in the manager’s absence

paragraphs.knowledge: Shift leaders maintain quality, service and cleanliness during their assigned period and coordinate staffing, stock, costs and customer responses. Confirm the restaurant’s decision limits and matters to report to the manager. Along with QSCA, concern for others’ happiness and difficulties should extend to coworkers as well as customers.
paragraphs.procedure: Plan from sales forecasts and issues, assign staff and tasks and execute. Observe quality and waiting times during service, then compare results and adjust afterwards. Connect yearly, monthly, weekly and daily plans. Reports to superiors include abnormalities, actions, unresolved matters and requests for the next shift as well as results.
paragraphs.mistakes: Short-term cost reductions from staffing cuts cannot sustain operations if poor service or accidents lose customers. Avoid taking everything on yourself or independently making changes beyond your authority. Base performance appraisal on concrete results, abilities and work behaviour rather than impressions alone.
paragraphs.scenario: Equipment fails while the manager is away. The shift leader stops use for safety and identifies dishes still available. Make staffing changes within your authority and seek manager approval for repair costs or service changes. Tell the next shift the faulty part, prohibited-use area and arrangements and request reopening checks.

rst-2-ops-01.summary: Understand your authority and connect planning, workplace observation, reporting and improvement.
rst-2-ops-01.activity: Read for 8 minutes and organise shift-leader decision limits in 7 minutes. Create a service-change report in 8 minutes and decide next-day verification points in 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-02.title: Interpret sales and labour-hour indicators
rst-2-ops-02.objective: Calculate indicators from sales, customers, gross profit and total working hours and explain their different meanings.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not confuse sales and gross profit

paragraphs.knowledge: Sales equal customer count × spending per customer; gross profit equals sales − cost of goods. Labour-hours are all employees’ actual working hours added together. Sales per labour-hour = sales ÷ total working hours; customers per labour-hour = customer count ÷ total working hours; labour-hour productivity = gross profit ÷ total working hours. Compare identical periods and conditions, including tax treatment.
paragraphs.procedure: For practice, use sales of 180,000 yen, 150 customers, costs of 54,000 yen and 36 total working hours. Spending per customer is 1,200 yen, gross profit 126,000 yen, sales per labour-hour 5,000 yen and labour-hour productivity 3,500 yen. Customers per labour-hour are about 4.17, rounded to two decimal places. Spending per customer and customers per labour-hour also let you verify sales per labour-hour.
paragraphs.mistakes: Even with equal sales per labour-hour, greater food loss lowers gross profit and labour-hour productivity. The labour distribution ratio is labour costs ÷ gross profit × 100, unlike the labour cost ratio whose denominator is sales. Set targets according to business type and restaurant plans; do not treat reference figures as universal obligations or wage standards.
paragraphs.scenario: Two stores have equal sales, but one has lower gross profit. Before reducing staff numbers, the supervisor checks costs, waste and product mix. Also examine service productivity and waits and choose improvements that reduce loss while maintaining sales. Do not use indicators solely to rush workers.

rst-2-ops-02.summary: Distinguish denominators and units and evaluate sales, gross profit and service together.
rst-2-ops-02.activity: Read for 8 minutes and recalculate the example in 8 minutes. Compare indicators when costs change for 7 minutes and explain the difference between labour distribution and labour cost ratios in 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-03.title: Investigate standard-versus-actual cost differences
rst-2-ops-03.objective: Calculate costs from stocktakes and sales records and analyse causes with explicit signs for differences.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Starting points for standard and actual costs
paragraphTitles.procedure: Write the difference definition before calculating
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not call every difference waste

paragraphs.knowledge: Standard cost is calculated from specified portions and purchase unit prices. Monthly standard cost totals each item’s units sold × standard cost per dish. Actual cost = previous month-end stock value + current purchases − current month-end stock value. Each cost ratio = that cost ÷ sales × 100; do not mix quantities and money.
paragraphs.procedure: Use sales of 1,000,000 yen, standard cost 300,000 yen, opening stock 120,000 yen, purchases 350,000 yen and closing stock 140,000 yen. Actual cost is 330,000 yen; standard and actual cost ratios are 30% and 33%. Loss expressed as actual minus standard is 30,000 yen and the ratio difference is +3 percentage points. Defined as standard minus actual, the cost-ratio variance is −3 points. State the name and sign explicitly.
paragraphs.mistakes: Cost differences can reflect overportioning, cooking or order errors, excess-stock disposal, inadequate receipt checks and stocktake quantity or price errors. A 3-point ratio difference differs from the relative percentage increase in cost. Source materials also vary in their definitions, so never omit the formula.
paragraphs.scenario: Costs rise despite little disposal. Checking deliveries and stocktakes, the supervisor finds a price per kg entered as a price per bag and corrects units and valuation. Separate real cost increases from recording errors and use distinct measures for portion checks and data-entry checks.

rst-2-ops-03.summary: Calculate standard and actual costs from separate records and state formulas, signs and percentage points when investigating causes.
rst-2-ops-03.activity: Read for 8 minutes and verify the example calculation in 8 minutes. Explain reversed variance-sign definitions in 7 minutes and create a cause-investigation sheet for rising costs in 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-04.title: Plan staffing from sales forecasts
rst-2-ops-04.objective: Estimate labour-hours from indicators and allocate staff with skills, breaks and busy periods considered.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Total hours differ from time-slot allocation
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not force workers just to balance numbers
paragraphTitles.scenario: An event increases only evening demand

paragraphs.knowledge: Estimate total working hours as planned sales ÷ target sales per labour-hour, or planned customers ÷ target customers per labour-hour. Even with equal totals, service stalls if skilled workers are lacking during busy periods. Forecast each period from weekdays, events, recent bookings and past results.
paragraphs.procedure: For example, planned sales of 240,000 yen divided by target sales per labour-hour of 4,000 yen gives 60 actual working hours. Allocate these to kitchen, dining area and washing, distinguishing breaks, cover, opening/closing and training time. When forecasts and results differ, revise allocations through discussion with staff and restaurant labour procedures.
paragraphs.mistakes: Plans that count work interruptions as breaks, require unrecorded preparation or place untrained staff in dangerous positions are inappropriate. Beyond reducing total hours, consider whether standardised preparation and improved movement can maintain service.
paragraphs.scenario: An event near the station increases evening bookings. Rather than increasing staffing evenly all day, the supervisor secures skilled staff for the rush and brings preparation and replenishment forward. Assign cover to ensure real breaks and compare forecasts, actual results and waits afterwards for next time.

rst-2-ops-04.summary: After calculating total hours, allocate by period considering skills, customer flow and breaks.
rst-2-ops-04.activity: Read for 8 minutes and create a 60-hour allocation in 8 minutes. Consider adjustments to changed demand in 7 minutes and check provision for breaks and training in 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-05.title: Connect ordering, stocktaking and receipt checks
rst-2-ops-05.objective: Decide order quantities from forecasts and actual stock and match purchase orders, delivery notes and goods.

paragraphTitles.procedure: Match actual stock and three quantities
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not sign after checking only the delivery note
paragraphTitles.scenario: Twelve bags arrive against ten ordered

paragraphs.knowledge: Too little stock loses sales through shortages; too much causes deterioration and ties up funds. Estimate needs from forecast sales, recipe quantities and time until the next delivery. Set buffer stock according to forecast uncertainty rather than applying a textbook’s assumed percentage to every item.
paragraphs.procedure: Separate returned and defective goods and accurately count weights and units, including opened items. At closing stocktake, the counter and recorder cross-check units, quantities and prices. On delivery, compare ordered quantities, delivery notes and actual quantity and quality; check origin, specification, temperature, damage and date/time before storing appropriately.
paragraphs.mistakes: Even when delivery notes match actual goods, quantities above the order are an overdelivery. Accepting without checking a short delivery creates hidden costs. Watch unit and price copying errors, duplicate counting and mixing items awaiting return. Do not use problematic items; contact the supplier.
paragraphs.scenario: Ten bags were ordered but twelve arrive, with a twelve-bag delivery note and good quality. The supervisor identifies the excess and, considering forecasts and storage capacity, declines it and adjusts quantities and billing with the supplier. Explain to the new worker that receipt checks prevent excess as well as shortages and retain the record.

rst-2-ops-05.summary: Order from actual stock and forecasts and check all three: purchase order, delivery note and goods.
rst-2-ops-05.activity: Read for 8 minutes and calculate orders from forecasts in 8 minutes. Handle a quantity discrepancy in 7 minutes and practise cross-checking stocktake units, quantities and prices for 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-06.title: Evaluate promotions and repeat visits
rst-2-ops-06.objective: Assess initiatives through sales volume, profit and customer response and improve relationships.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Volume alone does not establish success
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not remove items by classification alone

paragraphs.knowledge: Sales change through both customer count and spending per customer. Seasonal menus, sets, time discounts, points, reservations, takeaway, delivery and electronic payments serve different purposes. Repeat visits require quality, service and suitable suggestions. Distinguish discount effects on sales from effects on profit.
paragraphs.procedure: ABC analysis ranks items by a selected measure such as sales value or volume and classifies them by cumulative share. Decide the measure and boundaries first. Compare customer count, spending, gross profit, service time and waste under equal conditions before and after an initiative, checking regular, occasional and new customer responses.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not remove menus solely from classification: a low-selling item can be why particular customers visit. Discounts can increase orders while high food costs or delivery fees reduce profit. Remember regulars’ preferences without revealing personal visit history before companions. Respect customer choice and avoid unwanted pressure selling.
paragraphs.scenario: Discounted set sales rise. The supervisor also checks substitution from regular items, gross profit and peak kitchen load. Longer waits lead to changes in set contents and selling periods. Promote return visits at payment and track next month’s visits and profit before judging effectiveness.

rst-2-ops-06.summary: Set initiative purposes and comparison indicators and evaluate profit, workload and repeat visits too.
rst-2-ops-06.activity: Read for 8 minutes and classify the sales mix of five products in 8 minutes. Decide discount evaluation criteria in 7 minutes and practise considerate guidance for regulars in 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-07.title: Manage working hours, breaks and wages
rst-2-ops-07.objective: Record actual attendance and distinguish overtime, night work, statutory-holiday work and breaks.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not change records because it is busy
paragraphTitles.scenario: Help is requested during a break

paragraphs.knowledge: Scheduled hours may differ from time actually worked under employer direction. Preparation, tidying and training may need recording as work according to their content. Overtime, night work and statutory-holiday work have different classifications and premiums; the manager must report accurately to attendance and payroll staff.
paragraphs.procedure: Check the restaurant’s system, labour-management agreements, scheduled hours, statutory holidays and breaks and record actual starts and finishes. Provide cover so workers can leave duties and rest during shifts. Legal hour limits and premiums involve exceptions, overlaps and revisions: verify current official information and applicability before use.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not order tidying after clock-out, treat time worked during breaks as rest or alter actual records to match the schedule. Paying premiums does not permit ignoring overtime limits or agreements. Consult labour staff when unsure.
paragraphs.scenario: A worker briefly serves customers during a break due to a rush. The supervisor records the interruption and ensures the necessary break is provided again. Afterwards, review staffing and cover to prevent repetition and accurately report actual work and rest to payroll.

rst-2-ops-07.summary: Record actual work accurately and manage breaks and overtime categories according to applicable conditions.
rst-2-ops-07.activity: Read for 8 minutes and organise a planned-versus-actual work example in 8 minutes. Explain interrupted-break responses in 7 minutes and list questions for labour staff in 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-08.title: Paid leave, recruitment and first-day onboarding
rst-2-ops-08.objective: Check management suited to employment conditions and prepare new workers to begin safely.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Check conditions and the person’s wishes
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not refuse leave on personal judgement
paragraphTitles.scenario: New worker’s requested hours differ from the schedule

paragraphs.knowledge: Annual paid leave varies with continuous service, attendance, scheduled days and hours and other conditions. Check grants and use in the register and pass requests appropriately to the responsible department. In recruitment, confirm desired roles, availability and job requirements and explain restaurant conditions rather than imposing them unilaterally.
paragraphs.procedure: Follow approval procedures for hiring decisions and clearly communicate employment conditions. On the first day, explain clocking in/out, uniforms, hygiene, handwashing and emergency contacts, give a tour and introduce responsible staff. Explain training plans and tasks not yet permitted alone and designate someone for questions.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not independently say there is no paid leave because staffing is short or that all workers with few days are ineligible. Check laws and the responsible department for decisions such as timing. Do not put newcomers into busy posts without explanation and blame only them when they cannot perform.
paragraphs.scenario: On arrival, a new worker says the hours differ from those explained. The supervisor checks recruitment records and conditions, listens and asks the hiring team to coordinate. Meanwhile, prioritise explanation and safety training and clarify changed conditions and the trainer.

rst-2-ops-08.summary: Verify leave and conditions through records and systems and organise first-day explanations and a trainer.
rst-2-ops-08.activity: Read for 8 minutes and make a first-day guide in 8 minutes. Practise listening to a conditions mismatch for 7 minutes and organise paid-leave contacts and required information in 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-09.title: Design OJT and verify learning
rst-2-ops-09.objective: Specify purpose, method, tools, sequence, scope, quality and time and teach in four stages.

paragraphTitles.scenario: A newcomer is taught differently each time

paragraphs.knowledge: Before instruction, clarify the task’s purpose, method, tools, steps, scope, finished quality and standard time. Combine workplace skill learning through OJT with OFFJT for knowledge and thinking away from work. Practise posture, facial expression, volume and intonation as well as service words.
paragraphs.procedure: First explain the purpose and prepare the learner. Next demonstrate while explaining reasons. Then have the learner perform while observing steps and movements. Finally give specific feedback on successes and issues and arrange further practice and later checks. Divide long tasks and verify learning one-to-one.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not assign independent work merely because someone watched a video or said yes. Do not let wrong steps repeat: stop safely and teach immediately. Assess purpose, quality and safety rather than speed alone. If instructors teach differently, reorganise from the standard.
paragraphs.scenario: A newcomer is confused by different methods from different instructors. The supervisor aligns cleaning standards among instructors: tools, scope and finished condition. One instructor demonstrates, observes the learner and checks again the next day and after one week. Record mastered tasks and those needing further teaching.

rst-2-ops-09.summary: Progress to independent work through standard explanation, demonstration, learner performance and specific verification.
rst-2-ops-09.activity: Read for 8 minutes and organise seven elements of a cleaning task in 7 minutes. Practise four-stage teaching for 8 minutes and design next-day and one-week learning checks in 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-10.title: Prepare fire prevention and disaster responses
rst-2-ops-10.objective: Assign inspection, reporting and evacuation roles and protect customers and staff without dangerous independent actions.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not generalise dangerous firefighting or escape actions

paragraphs.knowledge: Fire arises from combustible material, oxygen and heat together. Manage kitchen oil, dirty ducts and gas or electrical faults, and maintain escape passages, guide lights and fire equipment. Fire-management roles, plans and training conditions depend on the building and store: check current fire-authority guidance.
paragraphs.procedure: Safely inspect flames, gas hoses, hoods, detectors and distribution boards and refer faults to specialists. Assign emergency calling, customer evacuation, equipment shutdown and staff checks and communicate exits and assembly points. During drills, check extinguisher fire compatibility and use and teach when evacuation takes precedence over initial firefighting.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not put water on oil fires or carry burning containers. Limit firefighting to trained methods, suitable equipment and circumstances where escape remains possible. Do not repeat old examples without their conditions or return into smoke. Evacuate if flames spread, smoke thickens or other danger is felt, and follow 119 instructions.
paragraphs.scenario: A worker raises the alarm when smoke emerges from the kitchen. The supervisor assigns calling and evacuation to different people. Check heat-source shutdown only as safely possible and guide guests away from smoke. At assembly, tell firefighters numbers and any missing-person information and prevent returns for belongings. After drills, correct communication and guidance delays.

rst-2-ops-10.summary: Prepare routine checks and roles and prioritise early reporting and safe evacuation in a fire.
rst-2-ops-10.activity: Read for 8 minutes and create routes and roles in 8 minutes. Practise emergency-call content for 7 minutes and explain prohibited actions for oil fires and smoke for 7 minutes.

rst-2-hyg-15.title: Organise appointment and duties of the food hygiene responsible person
rst-2-hyg-15.objective: Distinguish qualifications from internal authority and incorporate appointment, advice and training into operations.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Do not confuse job titles with statutory qualifications
paragraphTitles.scenario: Hand over the implementation system at changeover

paragraphs.knowledge: Ordinary restaurants designate a food hygiene responsible person. A title such as manager or head chef alone does not meet qualification requirements. Current rules include people meeting food sanitation inspector or food sanitation manager qualifications, holders of listed professional qualifications and graduates of training conducted or recognised by prefectural governors or equivalent authorities. A food sanitation manager, when appointed, may also serve in this role.
paragraphs.procedure: Professional qualifications include cook, confectionery hygiene specialist and nutritionist; current rules also explicitly include registered dietitian. Ships’ cooks, slaughterhouse hygiene-management and work-hygiene responsible persons, and poultry-processing hygiene managers are also listed. Check certificates and training completion documents and follow local public health centre appointment/change procedures. Do not extend exceptions for particular businesses to restaurants generally.
paragraphs.mistakes: The food hygiene responsible person manages hygiene under the operator’s direction and communicates necessary cautions and improvement opinions; the operator respects those opinions. According to business category, also endeavour to update knowledge through practical training. Assign on-site contacts and implementers so checks continue on absence days. Borrowing qualifications does not replace actual duties.
paragraphs.scenario: The responsible person is leaving. The manager checks the successor’s qualifications, necessary procedures and handover of hygiene plans and abnormality records rather than just recording a job title. An outstanding cooling-equipment improvement requires clear approvers and completion checkers, with the decision history passed to the successor.

rst-2-hyg-15.summary: Check qualifications and appointment procedures and build a system that implements and verifies advice. Also compare qualification wording in old materials and current rules.
rst-2-hyg-15.activity: Read for 9 minutes and inspect qualification documents for three fictional candidates in 7 minutes. Make a resignation/changeover handover sheet in 7 minutes and explain the operator’s response to improvement advice in 7 minutes.

rst-2-hyg-16.title: Plan food-sample scope, collection and storage
rst-2-hyg-16.objective: Distinguish large-volume service sample requirements and storage methods and retain traceable raw and cooked samples.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not call all storage conditions universal law

paragraphs.knowledge: Here, retained food samples means preserving ingredients and cooked food to investigate food poisoning, not tasting food. Implementing rules require storage and service records for operators preparing and serving the same food at least 300 meals at once or 750 meals per day. Smaller operations may also have local guidance or facility standards: do not decide samples are unnecessary from numbers alone.
paragraphs.procedure: The large-scale catering hygiene manual specifies about 50 g each of raw ingredients and cooked foods by type, sealed separately in clean containers and kept at −20°C or below for at least 2 weeks. Collect raw ingredients in their purchased state before washing or disinfection. Identify menu, collection date/time, ingredient lot and collector, and confirm cooked-food samples are taken after cooking.
paragraphs.mistakes: Learn 50 g and −20°C as methods in the manual for applicable facilities rather than universal statutory conditions for every restaurant. A freezer setting alone does not verify actual storage temperature. Mixing dishes in one bag or disinfecting raw samples first loses investigative clues. Do not confuse stored specimens with ingredients for service.
paragraphs.scenario: A plan delivers 360 identical boxed meals at once. The person in charge checks applicability and assigns raw/cooked sample collection, freezer space and storage-end-date checks. Record destination, serving or dispatch time and quantity. Do not assume leftovers are enough: confirm required collection before dispatch.

rst-2-hyg-16.summary: Check service scale and facility guidance and link retained food with destinations, dates, times and quantities.
rst-2-hyg-16.activity: Spend 8 minutes deciding applicability, 8 minutes planning raw and cooked sample collection, 7 minutes drafting bag labels and 7 minutes practising reports of temperature deviations or missed collection.

rst-2-hyg-17.title: Inspect 14 general-hygiene areas with a monitoring sheet
rst-2-hyg-17.objective: Match the 14 management areas with implementation records and find omissions hidden by scores.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Unify the 14 areas into a hygiene system
paragraphTitles.procedure: Find evidence in items and records
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not turn reference scores into pass criteria
paragraphTitles.scenario: Many records can still leave gaps

paragraphs.knowledge: General hygiene management covers 14 areas: responsible person, facilities, equipment, water, rodents/insects, waste/drainage, handlers, retained food samples, information, recall/disposal, transport, sale, training and other records. A transport abnormality, for example, connects not just to transport but also information, sales suspension and recall controls.
paragraphs.procedure: For each area, identify actual tasks, responsible person, implementation date and verification record. Check links between the hygiene plan, needed procedures, training, records and periodic review. For important processes, trace hazard analysis, critical control points, critical limits, monitoring, corrective action, verification and records in sequence.
paragraphs.mistakes: The food sanitation monitoring sheet at the end of the materials is a reference for management status, not the app mock-exam scoring table. Do not mark non-applicable items satisfactory on your own or claim an on-site inspection from documents alone. For missing items, check reasons and applicability and add needed work to the plan.
paragraphs.scenario: A restaurant has cleaning and temperature sheets but nobody assigned to update allergens when ingredients change. An inspector identifies weak information provision and assigns people to connect purchasing changes, kitchen checks and customer explanations. Complete the action only after matching actual labels with explanatory materials.

rst-2-hyg-17.summary: Check that planning, implementation, records and improvement connect across both the 14 areas and important processes.
rst-2-hyg-17.activity: Read for 8 minutes and create a fictional restaurant’s 14-area list in 8 minutes. Identify three evidence gaps in 7 minutes and set responsibilities, deadlines and rechecks in 7 minutes.

rst-2-hyg-18.title: Read food-poisoning statistics by year, incidents and patients
rst-2-hyg-18.objective: Distinguish historical textbook data from current figures and explain management issues using incident-versus-patient differences.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Rankings differ even within the same year
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not use past declines as safety guarantees

paragraphs.knowledge: The materials’ nationwide 2022 totals are 962 incidents and 6,856 patients. Leading incident counts are Anisakis 566, Campylobacter 185 and norovirus 63. By patient count, the order is norovirus 2,175, Clostridium perfringens 1,465, Campylobacter 822 and Salmonella 698.
paragraphs.procedure: Use total incidents as the denominator for incident shares and total people for patient shares. Norovirus incident share is 63 ÷ 962 × 100, about 6.5%; patient share is 2,175 ÷ 6,856 × 100, about 31.7%. These are rounded to one decimal place. Always include the aggregation scope and year.
paragraphs.mistakes: Movement restrictions, business conditions and differences in testing and reporting can affect statistics. Do not dismiss causes with few incidents or attribute a single year’s change conclusively to controls. Do not describe 2022 figures as this year’s latest. Compare annual publications using matching items and definitions.
paragraphs.scenario: A trainer looks only at leading incident counts and proposes teaching parasite controls alone. The supervisor also shows patient counts and explains the need for controls on human-mediated viral contamination and post-cooking cooling and storage. Build training from both statistics and workplace records matched to the restaurant’s menu and processes.

rst-2-hyg-18.summary: State years and denominators and do not directly equate statistical rankings with your restaurant’s risk ranking.
rst-2-hyg-18.activity: Spend 8 minutes reading, 8 minutes calculating incident and patient shares, 7 minutes explaining a graph including its year and 7 minutes planning training connected to restaurant processes.

rst-2-hyg-19.title: Manage detergent concentration, soaking and rinsing
rst-2-hyg-19.objective: Read conditions for detergents allowed on food and translate them into work without confusing times or targets.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Longer soaking is not necessarily better
paragraphTitles.scenario: Use two timers for different purposes

paragraphs.knowledge: Detergents for vegetables, fruit and tableware have product and concentration restrictions for each use. A neutral label alone does not establish suitability for food. Hand soap, alkaline products for heavy grease and acidic products for scale serve different purposes. Dishwashers need products suited to their model.
paragraphs.procedure: Even detergents permitted for vegetables and fruit require the specified concentration, and food must not remain soaking in solution for 5 minutes or longer. After detergent use, running-water rinsing guidance is at least 30 seconds for vegetables/fruit and 5 seconds for tableware. With standing-water rinsing, change the water and rinse at least twice. These are detergent rinsing conditions, separate from disinfectant contact times.
paragraphs.mistakes: Five minutes is not a minimum waiting time: food must not remain soaking for 5 minutes or longer. Correct timing without the correct concentration is insufficient. Do not mix acidic products with chlorine chemicals. Check protective equipment and instructions before handling chemicals and never use unsuitable products on food.
paragraphs.scenario: A new worker leaves vegetables in detergent to begin another task. The supervisor tracks soaking start to prevent prolonged exposure and times subsequent rinsing separately. The work sheet separates target, product name, concentration, soaking limit and rinse method, and understanding is checked through demonstration.

rst-2-hyg-19.summary: Follow product targets and conditions and do not reverse soaking limits and minimum rinse times.
rst-2-hyg-19.activity: Read conditions for 8 minutes, practise product selection for 7 minutes, create separate soaking/rinsing instructions for 8 minutes and explain the targets of 5 minutes, 30 seconds, 5 seconds and 2 rinses in 7 minutes.

rst-2-hyg-20.title: Distinguish heat, chemical and ultraviolet disinfection and checks
rst-2-hyg-20.objective: Choose disinfection for the utensil and manage effectiveness beyond lights being on or settings being correct.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not apply the roughly 3,000-hour example to all products
paragraphTitles.scenario: A disinfected label alone is insufficient

paragraphs.knowledge: Materials give examples of treating washed utensils at 80°C for at least 5 minutes or boiling heat-resistant parts and fabrics at 100°C for at least 5 minutes. The large-scale catering manual also gives 80°C for 5 minutes or an equally effective method. Not everything should be boiled: material, shape, equipment instructions and facility procedures are prerequisites.
paragraphs.procedure: Remove dirt, rinse, perform required treatment, dry and store hygienically as one sequence. Follow specified post-treatment for chlorine chemicals that corrode metal. Note that surface water dilutes alcohol. In UV cabinets, avoid shadowing through stacking, leave spacing for light to reach surfaces and follow equipment management conditions.
paragraphs.mistakes: UV germicidal lamps lose effective output even while lit. The material gives about 3,000 hours as a life guideline, but verify actual replacement times from manufacturer specifications and use conditions. Record illumination checks, cumulative hours, cleaning and replacement history; switch doubtful equipment to verified treatment. Do not expose eyes or skin directly.
paragraphs.scenario: Water remains in a bowl taken from a disinfection cabinet. The person in charge holds it from use and checks loading, drying and equipment history. Regularly check thermometers and chemical-measuring devices too, and return utensils only after seeing reprocessing results. Do not enter unmeasurable values as normal.

rst-2-hyg-20.summary: Distinguish example treatment conditions from actual specifications and connect washing, disinfection, drying, storage and checking.
rst-2-hyg-20.activity: Read for 8 minutes, choose methods for utensils of different heat resistance for 8 minutes, make a UV-equipment history sheet in 7 minutes and explain why a lit device may still fail in 7 minutes.

rst-2-hyg-21.title: Check water categories and inspection records
rst-2-hyg-21.objective: Understand water sources and tanks and manage testing, equipment checks and abnormality shutdown under applicable conditions.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Do not decide management from a water label alone
paragraphTitles.procedure: Set test dates and report-retention deadlines
paragraphTitles.mistakes: One measurement does not cover every parameter
paragraphTitles.scenario: Moving into a building with a receiving tank

paragraphs.knowledge: Food water is generally supplied by a waterworks or equivalent service or is water suitable for drinking. Private dedicated water systems have conditions such as supplying over 100 residents or daily maximum domestic-water volume over 20 m³, with exceptions. Even tanks receiving only mains water are treated differently for small systems and simplified dedicated systems above 10 m³ effective capacity. Confirm the category with facility management.
paragraphs.procedure: For water suitable for drinking, implementing rules require quality testing at least once a year. Keep reports for 1 year, or the longer period when food takes at least a year to be used or consumed. Additional tests are needed if disaster may contaminate the source. Clean tanks regularly and, where disinfection or purification equipment is installed, check operation and record results.
paragraphs.mistakes: The 0.1 mg/L free-residual-chlorine figure applies in water-supply hygiene management or applicable facility procedures. It alone does not guarantee all safety of food-use water. Check test-paper type and units. Do not taste suspicious water with odour, cloudiness or post-disaster concerns: stop use and consult.
paragraphs.scenario: Moving into a building with a receiving tank, the manager does not assume mains supply means nothing is needed. Check tank capacity, cleaning records, test reports and responsibilities through to the restaurant taps. Assess ice-making and cooking effects and consult building management and the public health centre on needed tests at actual outlets.

rst-2-hyg-21.summary: Check source and equipment categories and manage routine and abnormality testing, test reports and equipment records separately.
rst-2-hyg-21.activity: Create a water route diagram in 8 minutes, check annual testing and report-retention periods in 7 minutes, assign report/tank-cleaning/equipment-check roles in 8 minutes and practise disaster shutdown contacts for 7 minutes.

rst-2-hyg-22.title: Manage pests through frequency, surveys and records
rst-2-hyg-22.objective: Distinguish twice-yearly extermination from survey-based methods and plan source removal and record retention.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not create new chemical contamination

paragraphs.knowledge: Implementing rules generally require rodent and insect extermination at least twice a year and keeping implementation records for 1 year. Alternatively, methods and frequency suited to the facility can be chosen if regular systematic surveys of occurrence, habitats, entry routes and damage support effective measures. An impression of not seeing pests does not replace a survey.
paragraphs.procedure: For flies, distinguish outside entry from breeding in drains or rubbish. For cockroaches, inspect warm equipment and crevices; for rodents, trace access through pipes, doors and ceilings and food damage. Maintain screens, traps and drain covers and keep food and packaging away from floors and walls. Cover opened products and reduce food, water and hiding places.
paragraphs.mistakes: Agree pesticide type, location, food protection, carcass removal and reopening checks with specialists. Do not spray near food being prepared. Avoid placing insect-attracting lamps where visible outside and drawing pests in. Record dates, survey locations, results, actions and checkers; do more than simply receive contractor reports.
paragraphs.scenario: A restaurant uses regular surveys, but captures increase in the wash area. Rather than wait for the next extermination date, the supervisor investigates drainage and cleaning and consults a specialist for additional measures. Track captures after treatment to verify effects and retain reasons for changing survey locations or frequency.

rst-2-hyg-22.summary: Distinguish default frequency from alternative-method conditions and connect surveys, actions and effectiveness through records.
rst-2-hyg-22.activity: Check rule conditions for 8 minutes, map survey points for flies, cockroaches and rodents for 8 minutes, choose actions from results for 7 minutes and plan 1-year records and rechecks for 7 minutes.

rst-2-cook-09.title: Explain four wagyu breeds and Japanese origin labels
rst-2-cook-09.objective: Distinguish wagyu breeds from Japanese-raised beef and give explanations supported by purchasing documents.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not infer brands from region or coat colour

paragraphs.knowledge: Wagyu includes Japanese Black, Japanese Brown, Japanese Polled and Japanese Shorthorn and crosses among them. Being raised in Japan alone does not prove a wagyu breed. Marbling is fat distributed within meat and one quality factor; do not collapse breed, origin, individual animal, cut and rearing conditions into one word.
paragraphs.procedure: Japanese Black was improved through crossing with breeds including Brown Swiss, and Japanese Brown with breeds including Simmental. Japanese Shorthorn has roots in Tohoku native cattle crossed with Shorthorn, and Japanese Polled in native cattle crossed with Aberdeen Angus. Known production areas include Kumamoto/Kochi for Brown, Iwate for Shorthorn and Yamaguchi for Polled. Verify actual goods from delivery documents.
paragraphs.mistakes: Textbook rearing proportions are historical and must not be presented as current herd numbers. Do not identify wagyu or a brand from colour or marbling alone. Regional traditional varieties also exist for eggplant, butterbur, onions, burdock, udo, radish, turnip, crown daisy and beans, but a similar name does not establish regional certification.
paragraphs.scenario: Ordered beef is unavailable and another Japanese-raised beef will be used. The supervisor checks breed, cut and origin with the supplier rather than assuming domestic means the same wagyu. Review dish standards, price and menu explanations and share verified changed information with service staff.

rst-2-cook-09.summary: Verify breed, origin, brand and cut separately and do not treat Japanese-raised and wagyu as synonyms.
rst-2-cook-09.activity: Organise the four breeds for 8 minutes, match purchasing documents for 8 minutes, check traditional-vegetable explanations for 7 minutes and practise kitchen/service contact about substitutes for 7 minutes.

rst-2-cook-10.title: Read additive categories and sweetening, preservation and colour functions
rst-2-cook-10.objective: Separate regulatory categories from functional names and check labels and use standards when selecting processed goods.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Functions alone do not determine foods or quantities

paragraphs.knowledge: Regulatory categories include designated additives, existing additives, natural flavourings and ordinary food additives. Current Consumer Affairs Agency guidance says designated additives are designated by the Prime Minister. Do not present the materials’ Health Minister explanation or counts of 475 designated and 357 existing additives as of 26 July 2023 as the current authority or latest totals.
paragraphs.procedure: Sweeteners add sweetness, with xylitol and aspartame as examples. Colours include gardenia yellow and Food Yellow No. 4. Preservatives such as sorbic acid and sodium benzoate inhibit microbial growth. Colour-fixing agents sodium nitrite and sodium nitrate affect meat-product colour and similar properties.
paragraphs.mistakes: Bleaching examples include sodium sulfite and sodium dithionite; antifungal agents include orthophenylphenol and diphenyl. Even approved additives differ in permitted foods, quantities and residue limits. Do not judge safety from natural-versus-synthetic impressions or treat food-use and equipment-use chemicals alike.
paragraphs.scenario: Two sauces have the same colour but different additive and ingredient labels. The manager compares labels, specifications, allergens, usage and storage rather than assuming identical contents. Use functional examples for understanding and verify actual composition and permissions with current specifications and supplier materials.

rst-2-cook-10.summary: Separate administrative categories from technical functions and check current systems, product labels and use conditions together.
rst-2-cook-10.activity: Study regulatory categories for 8 minutes, match sweeteners, colours, preservatives and colour-fixing agents for 8 minutes, check bleaching and antifungal uses for 7 minutes and make a supplier-change comparison in 7 minutes.

rst-2-cook-11.title: Organise additive functions in texture, aroma and manufacturing
rst-2-cook-11.objective: Connect functions with examples and explain manufacturing and quality roles from food labels.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Taste and nutrition do not imply universal health effects
paragraphTitles.scenario: Consider a change to stabilise texture

paragraphs.knowledge: Pectin and sodium carboxymethylcellulose are examples for thickening, stabilising and gelling. Emulsifiers such as glycerol fatty-acid esters and plant lecithin maintain mixed water and oil. Tofu coagulants include magnesium chloride and glucono-delta-lactone; distinguish function and target food even for similar firming effects.
paragraphs.procedure: Antioxidants include sodium erythorbate and mixed vitamin E; gum bases include ester gum and chicle. Raising agents such as sodium bicarbonate and burnt alum expand dough, while flavourings such as orange flavouring and vanillin add aroma. Check purposes and avoid confusing chemicals used for other functions.
paragraphs.mistakes: Acidulants include citric and lactic acids; flavour enhancers include monosodium L-glutamate and disodium 5′-inosinate. Vitamin C and calcium lactate are examples for nutritional fortification, but their presence does not make food a disease treatment. One substance may serve different purposes: return to labels and specifications to verify.
paragraphs.scenario: An unstable dessert leads to a proposal to increase thickener. The supervisor first examines ingredients, weighing, heating and cooling rather than solving through additive quantity alone. For changes, check food-specific standards and product instructions and approve after trials and label review. Do not add without limits on restaurant discretion.

rst-2-cook-11.summary: Distinguish texture, quality preservation, flavour, manufacturing and nutrition purposes and match examples with actual labels.
rst-2-cook-11.activity: Classify functions for 8 minutes, organise example cards for 10 functions for 9 minutes, compare labels for 6 minutes and explain recipe-change checks for 7 minutes.

rst-2-svc-09.title: Design location-specific dining-area cleaning procedures
rst-2-svc-09.objective: Use source work examples to reconstruct your restaurant’s procedures by area, material, tools, frequency and verification.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Reference dilution is not a universal recipe
paragraphTitles.scenario: Return missed areas to the frequency plan

paragraphs.knowledge: Manage rubbish and soil around the perimeter and planting, fingerprints on windows, mirrors and display cases, sand and water at entrances/passages and dirt between carpet fibres. Chairs, tables, counters, partitions, telephones, tills, seasoning containers, washrooms and toilets differ in food contact and touch frequency. Do not reuse one area’s tools everywhere.
paragraphs.procedure: Collect perimeter rubbish, loosen window dirt, remove water and dry frames. Remove sand before appropriately wiping floors without leaving slip hazards. Handle seasoning contents according to restaurant procedures, then wash, rinse and dry containers. Clearly separate toilet brushes, toilet mops and dining cloths and include handwashing after use.
paragraphs.mistakes: The textbook cleaning table is one example. Do not apply dilution ratios such as 20-fold or application distances to other products or materials unchanged. Follow detergent concentration and rinsing instructions. Do not spray liquid directly on phones or tills: check equipment instructions. Confirm materials and manufacturer conditions for carpet, furniture wax and similar products too.
paragraphs.scenario: Passages are clean daily, but mirrors and seasoning-container rims remain dirty. The manager separates daily checks, as-needed actions and after-service disassembly cleaning and defines responsibilities and finish standards. Recheck washrooms on rounds and arrange water, chemicals and tools during service to avoid contact and fall hazards.

rst-2-svc-09.summary: Set methods and finished conditions for each target and distinguish reference concentrations/frequencies from product and restaurant conditions.
rst-2-svc-09.activity: Check 12 targets for 8 minutes, make four procedures for dining areas, windows, seasonings and toilets in 9 minutes, separate tools for 6 minutes and check service-time safety and completion for 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-11.title: Assess statutory hours, breaks and days off numerically
rst-2-ops-11.objective: Judge thresholds under ordinary working-time rules and confirm exceptions and variable-hour systems when scheduling.

paragraphs.knowledge: Ordinary statutory hours are generally 8 per day and 40 per week. Certain commerce, cinema/theatre, health/hygiene and hospitality/entertainment workplaces regularly employing fewer than 10 workers have a 44-hour week and 8-hour day exception. Restaurants are not automatically eligible: check headcount and applicability with labour staff, including part-time workers.
paragraphs.procedure: Daily work over 6 and up to 8 hours requires at least 45 minutes’ break; over 8 hours requires at least 1 hour. Distinguish exactly 6 from over 6. Days off are generally at least 1 per week, or check the starting date and number under a lawful 4-days-in-4-weeks system. Include directed preparation, tidying and training in actual working time.
paragraphs.mistakes: Even the 44-hour exception does not automatically extend the 8-hour daily limit. Variable working-time systems require procedures and prior schedules; changing records after a busy day cannot establish one. Workers under 18 and others have further restrictions. Do not shift breaks to before starting or immediately before leaving and claim a genuine mid-work break.
paragraphs.scenario: Someone scheduled for 6 actual hours will work 30 minutes longer. The supervisor recognises that actual work exceeds 6 hours and provides cover for a break rather than retaining the original no-break schedule. If another day may exceed 8 hours, secure at least 1 total break hour and record interrupted customer-service time as work, not rest.

rst-2-ops-11.summary: Separate daily/weekly limits, breaks according to actual hours and days-off systems and verify exceptions before scheduling.
rst-2-ops-11.activity: Read rules for 8 minutes, decide breaks for 6, 6½ and 8½ hours of work in 8 minutes, compare 40-hour and exceptional 44-hour weeks for 7 minutes and revise a schedule including cover in 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-12.title: Separate overtime, night and statutory-holiday premiums
rst-2-ops-12.objective: Distinguish premium applicability and overlaps and give payroll accurate attendance categories.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Distinguish premium rates from total payments
paragraphTitles.procedure: Total the portion above 60 monthly hours separately
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Not every day off is the same category
paragraphTitles.scenario: The same base wage gives different totals by hours

paragraphs.knowledge: Ordinary statutory overtime premium is at least 25%, night work from 22:00 to 05:00 at least 25%, and statutory-holiday work at least 35%. Overtime plus night work gives at least 50%, holiday plus night at least 60%. These are additions to base wages, not total payment of only 25%.
paragraphs.procedure: The portion of monthly statutory overtime above 60 hours carries at least 50%, or 75% when overlapping night work. This also applies to small and medium enterprises from April 2023. Exclude statutory-holiday work from the 60-hour total. Work on scheduled non-statutory days off that qualifies as overtime is classified and totalled separately; check the month’s start and attendance settings.
paragraphs.mistakes: Sunday is not automatically a statutory holiday and a manager title does not automatically exempt premiums. Do not add overtime’s 25% to statutory-holiday work; check holiday and night categories. Systems such as substitute leave under labour-management agreements have separate conditions. Do not erase unpaid premiums through arbitrary leave: ask labour staff.
paragraphs.scenario: For practice, use a base hourly amount of 1,200 yen. Ordinary overtime is at least 1,500 yen and overtime plus night at least 1,800 yen. Monthly overtime beyond 60 hours overlapping night is at least 2,100 yen. In practice, check included allowances, applicable systems and rounding with payroll too.

rst-2-ops-12.summary: Classify hours first and apply the conditions for 25%, 35%, 50%, 60% and 75% separately from base wages.
rst-2-ops-12.activity: Check classifications for 8 minutes, make a night-overlap table in 8 minutes, calculate from a 1,200-yen base for 7 minutes and practise separating statutory holidays from the monthly 60-hour total for 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-13.title: Check Article 36 agreements and overtime limits
rst-2-ops-13.objective: Distinguish premium pay from the procedure for extending working hours, and check the standard limits and what each special-clause calculation includes.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Paying more does not automatically permit longer hours
paragraphTitles.procedure: Check the limits that still apply under a special clause
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not make the maximum your working-hours target
paragraphTitles.scenario: Adjust staffing early using attendance forecasts

paragraphs.knowledge: Work beyond statutory hours or on statutory holidays generally requires procedures such as concluding and filing an Article 36 agreement. The usual overtime limits are 45 hours per month and 360 hours per year. Different limits apply to certain systems, including some annual variable working-hours systems, so check the system used at your restaurant. Do not treat chronic staff shortages as temporary circumstances.
paragraphs.procedure: Even with a special clause for exceptional temporary circumstances, overtime is generally limited to 720 hours per year. Overtime plus holiday work must total less than 100 hours in any month, and each average over 2–6 months must be no more than 80 hours. Overtime may exceed 45 hours in a month for no more than 6 months per year. Holiday work is treated differently in the 720-hour annual calculation and in the monthly 100-hour and average 80-hour calculations.
paragraphs.mistakes: A special clause is not a system for making employees work up to the limit every month. Premium pay alone cannot make up for the absence of an Article 36 agreement, and having an agreement does not remove the need to manage health and breaks. Do not casually apply exemptions or rules for other types of work to ordinary restaurant employees. If a limit is approaching, seek advice before assigning the work.
paragraphs.scenario: Before month-end, overtime is approaching the standard limit. The person in charge checks remaining reservations and preparation volumes, and considers extra support, standardizing tasks, and adjusting the range of service. They confirm the agreement’s application and cumulative hours with the labor administrator, then revise assignments to what can safely be worked without rewriting actual attendance to show fewer hours than planned.

rst-2-ops-13.summary: Check extension procedures, limit calculations, and premium pay separately; act on forecasts without falsifying actual records.
rst-2-ops-13.activity: Read for 8 minutes; organize the conditions for 45, 360, and 720 hours for 7 minutes; compare the holiday-inclusive limits of less than 100 hours and an average no more than 80 hours for 8 minutes; propose adjustments to schedules nearing a limit for 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-14.title: Read paid-leave entitlement tables and leave-taking duties
rst-2-ops-14.objective: Choose entitlement from the table using service length and working conditions, and correctly manage rescheduling and the annual 5-day leave-taking requirement.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Check eligibility and the general entitlement
paragraphTitles.procedure: Choose the proportional table using working conditions
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not reduce leave merely because a job is called part-time
paragraphTitles.scenario: The same 4-day week can use different tables

paragraphs.knowledge: Annual paid leave arises after 6 months of continuous employment with attendance on at least 80% of all working days in that period. Continue checking attendance and other requirements for each subsequent qualifying period. General entitlements are 10 days after 0.5 years of service, 11 after 1.5 years, 12 after 2.5, 14 after 3.5, 16 after 4.5, 18 after 5.5, and 20 after 6.5 years or more.
paragraphs.procedure: Use proportional entitlement for eligible employees, such as those working less than 30 hours and no more than 4 days per week. In service-length order of 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5, 5.5, and 6.5 years or more, a 4-day week [169–216 days/year] gives 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, and 15 days. A 3-day week [121–168 days/year] gives 5, 6, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 11 days. A 2-day week [73–120 days/year] gives 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, and 7 days. A 1-day week [48–72 days/year] gives 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, and 3 days.
paragraphs.mistakes: Also check conditions for the general table, such as at least 30 hours/week, 5 days/week, or 217 days/year. Employees granted at least 10 days of annual leave must generally take 5 days within 1 year from the entitlement date. Days taken at the employee’s request or under a planned leave arrangement count, so this does not mean adding another 5 days twice. Rescheduling a requested date because it would obstruct normal business operations is different from refusing annual leave itself.
paragraphs.scenario: New employee A works 4 days per week but has 32 scheduled weekly hours, so check application of the general table. B works 4 days and 24 hours per week and qualifies for proportional entitlement: 7 days after 6 months if the requirements are met. The supervisor checks employment records and attendance rates with the responsible department and records entitlement dates, remaining days, and leave taken in the register.

rst-2-ops-14.summary: Choose the table from scheduled hours and days, service length, and attendance—not a job label—and keep entitlement and leave-taking records distinct.
rst-2-ops-14.activity: Check the general table for 7 minutes; read the proportional tables for 4-, 3-, 2-, and 1-day weeks for 9 minutes; assess 3 people with different working conditions for 7 minutes; practice managing the annual 5-day requirement and responding to requests for 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-15.title: Check whether a fire prevention manager is required and appoint one
rst-2-ops-15.objective: Check the required arrangements using whole-building and tenant conditions, and compare qualifications with actual management authority.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Do not decide from seat numbers alone
paragraphTitles.procedure: Check qualifications and the position needed to perform the role
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not apply an old explanation uniformly to every restaurant

paragraphs.knowledge: For buildings that include uses open to the general public, such as restaurants, a total building occupancy of at least 30 people is a typical criterion for appointing a fire prevention manager. Different conditions apply in cases such as buildings containing residential facilities for people who have difficulty evacuating unaided. Even a restaurant with few seats may qualify because of the mixed-use building’s overall conditions; check building use and management divisions with the local fire department.
paragraphs.procedure: A fire prevention manager needs the position to manage and supervise, along with the necessary knowledge and skills. For qualifications such as course completion, check whether Class A or Class B is required for the building’s use and scale. Clarify who has management authority over the building and tenant premises, appointment and change notifications, and preparation of the fire defense plan. Avoid naming someone who has no authority to perform the work.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not conclude from a textbook’s phrase “for each restaurant” that every small restaurant has identical requirements. If the building as a whole is subject to requirements, tenant-side management is also needed. Additional local ordinance provisions or overall coordination may apply. Occupancy is not necessarily the number of customer seats; check the calculation method for each building use.
paragraphs.scenario: A small café moves into a mixed-use building with other occupancies. Rather than deciding that a small staff means no manager is needed, the person in charge consults building management and the fire department about overall use, occupancy, and qualification class. They reconcile written responsibilities for appointment, planning, drills, and evacuation routes, then check before opening that each person can actually act.

rst-2-ops-15.summary: Investigate building and tenant conditions, and use fire department guidance to confirm required qualifications, authority, notifications, and plans.
rst-2-ops-15.activity: Read for 8 minutes; compare a standalone restaurant and a mixed-use building for 8 minutes; prepare an authority and qualification checklist for 7 minutes; practice communication and handover when appointments change for 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-16.title: Manage fire prevention roles and drill records
rst-2-ops-16.objective: Link daily inspections, alarm and evacuation assignments, and improvements after drills to the fire defense plan.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Turn management duties into daily work
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not turn textbook demonstrations into actions by untrained people
paragraphTitles.scenario: Carry drill delays forward into the next plan

paragraphs.knowledge: Fire prevention planning covers the workplace fire response organization; firefighting, alarm, and evacuation drills; maintenance and inspection of required equipment; supervision of fire use; management of evacuation facilities; occupancy; training; emergency communication and guidance; and liaison with fire authorities. Make clear in advance who decides what and who takes over when an assigned person is absent.
paragraphs.procedure: Safely check deteriorating gas hoses, grease in hoods and ducts, dirty detectors, equipment operation, and abnormalities around distribution panels. Clear passageways and exits, and check exit signs and assembly points. Ask specialist contractors to dismantle or repair specialist equipment. Practice customer evacuation guidance, calling 119, safely stopping equipment where possible, and checking headcounts as separate roles.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not use methods such as covering an oil fire with a wet cloth or putting a bag over the face without checking the situation and relevant training. Do not pour water onto oil or carry a burning container. If smoke or fire is spreading and a safe escape route cannot be maintained, prioritize evacuation over firefighting. Do not let people return inside for belongings.
paragraphs.scenario: During a drill, the caller and evacuation guide compete for the same phone, delaying guidance. The supervisor separates the role assignments and revises absence cover and reporting after assembly. Record the drill date, participants, successes, improvements, and the next check. In a real fire, alert others by voice and prioritize early notification and safe evacuation.

rst-2-ops-16.summary: Do more than assign roles on paper: use inspections and drills to check people can act and support safe evacuation.
rst-2-ops-16.activity: Organize management tasks for 8 minutes; build a three-role assignment table for 8 minutes; check drill records and absence cover for 7 minutes; explain situations requiring an end to unsafe firefighting for 7 minutes.

rst-2-cook-12.title: Turn basic kitchen terms into production-plan instructions
rst-2-cook-12.objective: Use 20 kitchen terms in quality, inventory, and staffing instructions, specifying quantities and the required finished state.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Align product units and finished-product standards
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not leave layout and role terminology vague

paragraphs.knowledge: An item is one product or product type, while a portion is the quantity used for one serving. A recipe sets standards for ingredients, quantities, and steps; finished-product standards specify the target taste, amount, appearance, temperature, and time until service. After checking the glossary meanings, see whether your restaurant’s standards can be verified through numbers or actual examples.
paragraphs.procedure: Communicate conditions to suppliers through specification-based ordering and check delivered goods against them at receiving inspection. Verify quantities through stocktaking, and support freshness control with inventory management and first-in, first-out use. Central kitchens and kitchens using prepared food still need restaurant-level temperature, time, and hygiene checks. Forecast customers and sales, and use production control to adjust how much to make and when.
paragraphs.mistakes: Kitchen layout must reflect safety and contamination zones; do not confuse washing-area routes with cooking and serving routes. The pantry is a coordination point, not a place for leaving items unattended or chatting. Kitchen helpers also need defined duties and training. Do not infer ingredients or dietary restrictions from the category “ethnic food.” Changes over time do not justify extending storage periods.
paragraphs.scenario: The supervisor rewrites “prepare for the peak” into a sales forecast, required quantities, completion times, and holding conditions. They distinguish bussing used items from clearing unnecessary plates during the meal after confirming the customer’s wishes. Ask staff to repeat back and demonstrate instructions; check understanding of names separately from the ability to perform the task.

rst-2-cook-12.summary: Go beyond definitions: turn terms into instructions that make clear who does what, how much, and by when.
rst-2-cook-12.activity: Check the 20 glossary terms for 8 minutes; classify them into quality, inventory, layout, and production for 7 minutes; make 3 vague instructions specific for 8 minutes; explain how to verify performance through demonstration for 7 minutes.

rst-2-svc-10.title: Use basic service terms for observation and improvement
rst-2-svc-10.objective: Connect 20 customer-service terms to customer experience and workflow, and explain improvements suited to the restaurant.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Distinguish time-period terms from experience terms
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not turn selling terms into pressure to buy
paragraphTitles.scenario: Align terms with shared observation points

paragraphs.knowledge: Peak time is when customers concentrate; idle time is a relatively quiet period. Serving time runs from ordering until the food arrives, and textbook examples in minutes are not duties shared by every restaurant format. Visit frequency, customer segments, and CS help us understand customer experience, but must not be used to decide an individual’s wishes from appearance alone.
paragraphs.procedure: Customer routes differ between cafeteria-style service, where customers select food, and table service, where staff bring food to the table. Check dining-area layout, service stations, and table setting; coordinate meal progress when serving the same table’s dishes together. Side work includes cleaning and replenishing, but plan it so that it does not interfere with safety or customer care.
paragraphs.mistakes: Know core and promotional products, and use suggestive selling to offer choices that match the customer’s wishes. Improve cleanliness and hospitality through daily actions to encourage word of mouth and return visits. Handling complaints means listening, checking facts, and resolving issues—not recording only favorable comments.
paragraphs.scenario: When told “service is slow,” the supervisor separately observes the time from order to service, seating arrangement, and delays in replenishment. They check the service process for core products and whether dishes for one table arrive together. Compare waiting times and customer responses after improvements rather than ending with vague reflection expressed only in terminology.

terms.同時同卓提供: coordinated simultaneous service to the same table

rst-2-svc-10.summary: Use terms for shared observation, instruction, and improvement; do not turn reference values or categories into assumptions about customers.
rst-2-svc-10.activity: Check definitions of 20 terms for 8 minutes; compare service formats and routes for 7 minutes; break down a delay in an 8-minute exercise; choose before-and-after improvement indicators for 7 minutes.

rst-2-ops-17.title: Connect management terms to business decisions
rst-2-ops-17.objective: Link 20 management terms to planning, action, evaluation, and revision without confusing reference targets with legal duties.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Productivity measures can have different denominators
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not make textbook reference targets universal
paragraphTitles.scenario: Verify improvements through a management cycle

paragraphs.knowledge: Sales per labor-hour divides sales by total working hours; gross profit per labor-hour divides gross profit by total working hours. If labor productivity is measured as gross profit per person, align the period and how people are counted. The labor distribution ratio is labor costs as a share of gross profit; the cost ratio is costs as a share of sales. Do not confuse their denominators.
